Its faces print a true minus and no *−0.00%*, a rate under a tenth of a point to three places, and colour the verdicts and nothing else. `BankCheck`'s thirteenth section asserts the arithmetic the tab reads, and its section 13b, since 0.7.33, that every rung's parts are its rate — a sector's quote to the bit and an insured mortgage to 1e-12 at six dials — that a city just loaded quotes its record and its concentration, and that the branch verdict is the planner's. Since 0.7.74 Profit and the Balance sheet carry the sectors' *Summary | Statement* switch, one choice for both ([the screen](#22-the-screen)). The Statement is the bank's own format, because its income is interest: interest income by who paid it, less what it pays its savers and the window, to NET INTEREST INCOME; its fees, the trading desk and its gains on paper and bonds to TOTAL OPERATING INCOME; the provisions, its staff and its branches' upkeep, the tax a month in arrears, and what it paid out and kept. Its sheet is most liquid first, the deposits a memo, set against a year ago as the bank keeps its sheets; and its ratios are a bank's — net interest margin, cost to income, the fees' share, provisions of loans, return on equity and the payout; capital of the weighted book, equity of assets, loans of deposit funding, the liquid share, the allowance of loans and the overnight share. None of the redrawn tab has been seen on a screen.

## 15. The central bank

*Until 0.7.0 the game had a central bank, and it was the rest of the world. The commercial bank placed its spare cash abroad at the world's 2% and funded its shortfalls abroad; the policy dial only floored the lending rate on top, which is why it stopped mattering past 17%; and money was created only from outside — the founding, exports, capital coming in, the bank's wholesale funding — so the price level had nothing at home to answer to. Five batches, 0.6.11 to 0.7.3, brought the marginal role home, 0.7.15 made it the buyer of last resort for the city's paper, and 0.7.42 to 0.7.45 made what the city believes of it the anchor its prices are struck at. This is what the central bank is, what it holds, what each of its five dials does, how little the rate moved prices until 0.7.42 — measured, and said plainly — and the anchor that has it move them since.*

> **What was asked for**
>
> Jerus: *"…we implement a central bank, and basically the central bank would buy gbonds or sell gbonds from thin air … the feds sheet would show how much debt it holds, like debt to itself aka money printing, like QE and QT … and that is the M2 supply or what do you think?"* Decided the same night: a floor system, households who can hold the city's paper, and an autopilot beside the dial. Each batch was gated on the whole suite and on the eight seeds, and the design note that set them out is `the-central-bank.md`.

### The books

`CentralBank` is a balance sheet the player reads, on the Money page under Finances. **Assets:** advances to the commercial bank at the window; advances to the treasury, its overdraft, which is what "printed" means on the screens; the city's paper it holds, at face; and the vault, read from `ForeignAccounts` rather than moved there, because the treasury still buys and sells reserves and the currency's code has to see them. **Liabilities:** reserves and currency, which together are **M0**. Currency is zero — nobody in this city holds cash outside the bank — and kept so that the day somebody does it has a line. Its equity is what the two sides leave.

**Money is made and destroyed here and nowhere else.** An advance, interest on reserves and the remittance are money issued; a repayment, the window's interest and the advances' interest are money retired. `MoneyAudit` sees the central bank as a boundary participant, like the world, and declares both under a scope of its own, so the month's issued less retired is the change in M0 to the cent — the difference between money from thin air and a residual. `CentralBankCheck` section 1 walks a month with every kind of flow in it and asserts exactly that. M0 is a ledger of what this bank has made and not taken back, not a reading of the commercial bank's till, because money reaches the pools without passing through a central bank — exports, capital, the founding — and the two could not both hold the identity.

**M2** is what the public holds: the households' deposits, the sectors', the world's, and currency (`Game.getM2()`). It grows when the bank lends reserves on or the treasury spends printed money, not when the central bank buys from the bank. Both are series, with a column each in the year book. Since 0.7.32 the Money page draws the books as pictures: THE CENTRAL BANK'S BOOK as two bars on one scale, what it holds against what it owes, its equity the difference and a shortfall red; WHAT THE PUBLIC HOLDS, M2 as a bar of its parts; THIS MONTH, the money made and destroyed as bars of their parts and what M0 moved by; and M2 with M0, and the advances, as two small City History charts that open on ten years. On the default seed on 22 September the run ends with M0 at $2.39B, all of it reserves, M2 at $78.0B, the central bank having made $18.5B and destroyed $16.1B since founding and remitted $486M to the treasury — and its equity at minus $2.39B, a loss carried from paying interest on reserves in money it made, which is exactly what printing to pay interest on reserves looks like. On 0.7.2's eight default seeds it ended below zero in every one, at minus $1.1B to minus $3.3B. On 28 September, with the dial's median at 0.44% over the run, the default seed ended with M0 at $1.48M, M2 at $293.4B, $8.08B made and $8.08B destroyed since founding and $426M remitted, and its equity at $32.1M: the vault it counts as its asset, less $1.48M of loss carried. On 1 October, the dial's median 0.46%, it ended with M0 at $4.94M, M2 at $261.0B, $44.1M made and $39.1M destroyed since founding, nothing remitted over the run, and its equity at $13.9M, the vault less $4.94M of loss carried. On 5 October, at 0.7.49, the dial's median 3.18%, it ended with M0 at $173.2B, all of it reserves, M2 at $162.7T in a city whose prices had risen 1,213-fold, $173.2B made and nothing destroyed since founding, nothing remitted, and its equity at $221.7B, the vault less $173.2B of loss carried.

### The rate is a floor

The dial is the rate the central bank pays on reserves. The commercial bank's spare cash sits there earning it, where it used to earn the world's 2% abroad, and its shortfalls are borrowed at the **window** at the dial plus `WINDOW_PENALTY` — a quarter point since 0.7.7, the Bank of Canada's own spread, and a point before — where they used to cost the city's own paper rate plus two points and a stretch; a failed bank is charged nothing at the window while it is resolved (0.7.1), because its equity is zero and a charge would fail it again. Savers got their share of what reserves earned — a bank whose only income was its reserves paid them 0.675% at a 3% dial and 2.25% at 10%, the first time the dial had ever reached a household — and since 0.7.7 they get the share of the dial the bank chooses ([the bank](#14-the-bank)). Nothing lends below what reserves earn and nothing borrows above what the window charges, so the dial is the price of money: the city's note prices at its floor plus its spreads, and `MonetaryCheck`'s section 6 reads the city's rate at exactly the dial at 3, 10, 20 and 40% and the bank's lending rate about one to two points over it — 5.02%, 11.28%, 21.02% and 40.98% on 28 September, 5.00%, 11.27%, 20.99% and 40.93% on 1 October, and 4.99%, 11.27%, 21.00% and 40.94% on 5 October, at 0.7.49. On the way it found a premium counted twice: the carry trade and the bank's deposit bid were priced off a rate that already carried the strain premium, and `lendingRate()` added it again. The carry trade itself is untouched, and is now the priced alternative rather than the marginal source.

**Interest on reserves is paid in money made for it**, and that is the one place the floor has no floor of its own. Held at 30% or 50% for a whole run, M0 compounds to 10^8 to 3×10^14 $B while prices stay near one — spare cash earning the rate in new money that becomes spare cash — and the same mechanism took M0 to $1.25 quadrillion in the six broke seeds held at 0.7.1's stop of 25%. It is on the list.

**Autopilot.** A toggle on the monetary page hands the dial to the Taylor rule each month — the rule the page already prints, which since 0.7.2 is clamped only by the dial's bound at 100% — until the player's hand takes it back; saved, and held in a playtest by `-Dplaytest.autopilot`; the dial itself is held for a whole run by `-Dplaytest.policyRate`. With the rule on the dial on all eight seeds, 0.7.2 took bank failures from 27 to 17, the dial peaked at 30.5% and no seed spiralled: with the rule's hand on it, a credible real rate holds. Since 0.7.13 a new game founds on the autopilot; an older save keeps the hand it was played with.

**The target is the player's.** Jerus: *"i want to have the dial not target 0 inflation, set it so that you can choose what is your inflation target"*. Since 0.7.4 the rule aims at `inflationTarget`, 2% by default (`DEFAULT_INFLATION_TARGET`, the constant it had been), in half points from nothing to 10%, and since 0.7.15 to 20% — Jerus: *"inflation target can be higher tgan 10%, up yo 20%"* (`MAX_INFLATION_TARGET`). It sits under the autopilot on the monetary page and applies at once, like the ceiling, with chips to 5%, and the rule's sentence is struck live at the target and at another (`ruleRate(inflation, target)`), so that at 5% inflation the page can say the rule sets 7.5% aiming at 2% and 8.5% aiming at nothing without doing the arithmetic itself — 10.5% until 0.7.42. **On target the rule sets the neutral real rate plus the target** since 0.7.42: `NEUTRAL_RATE`'s 3% is the neutral nominal rate at the default 2%, a real rate of one point, so a 5% target is met on target at 6% and a 0% target at 1% (`DebtManager.ruleRate()`). Until then the rule read `NEUTRAL_RATE` + `TAYLOR_WEIGHT` × (inflation − target) whatever the target, which at a 20% target sat at the 0% floor until inflation passed 18% — a target the rule could not aim at, and part of the question 0.7.42 answered (below). At 2% the two are the same to the bit. It is saved under its own key, an older save reads 2%, and `-Dplaytest.inflationTarget` holds it for a run. The colours of the header's INFLATION tile read from it, as the strip's did until 0.7.21 ([the currency](#16-prices-the-currency--the-world)).

**So is how strictly it holds it**, since 0.7.52. Jerus, rather than chasing the ensemble's failing criteria: *"just a very simple fix, aka beside the target inflation, how strict, very strict then it trys to have it below the target, very loose and the target is a suggestion"*. A ladder of five steps sits under the target's on THE RULE card, set at once like it (`DebtManager.Strictness`), and each step is two numbers of the rule. A strict step aims under the target, the target taken as a ceiling and the rule struck at the aim as it would be at a target of the aim: **very strict** a point under (`STRICTEST_AIM`, which is `Expectations.TOLERANCE`, the furthest under the target that still counts as on it, so hitting the aim costs no trust), answering the gap at 2 (`STRICTEST_WEIGHT`), and never aiming under 0%, because no central bank aims at falling prices — so at a 0.5% target both strict steps aim at 0% and differ only in weight. A loose step lets inflation be inside a band either side of the target, holding the neutral rate there and answering only what is past it, so the rate never jumps at the band's edge: **very loose** two points each way (`LOOSEST_BAND`, so its outer point is a miss that trust counts and the bank does not answer), at 1.25 (`LOOSEST_WEIGHT`) — still over one, so past its band a point of inflation still makes money dearer. **Strict**, half a point under at 1.75, and **Loose**, a point each way at 1.375, sit halfway in both numbers, and **Standard** is the rule as it was, to the bit. One weight serves both sides, so a strict bank also cuts harder under its aim. At the default 2% target and on it, very strict sets 4.00%, strict 3.38% and the other three the neutral 3%; at 5% inflation the five set 10.00%, 8.63%, 7.50%, 5.75% and 4.25%. Trust is still judged on the target, and the lean that spares it is measured against what holding the target takes — the Standard rule's advice and the neutral rate, `holdingRate()` and `neutralRate()` — so a looser bank on the autopilot loses trust as far as it falls short, and a stricter one can lean no more than all the way. The card says, at the step under the thumb, what the bank aims at and what the rule would set on target and at this year's inflation (`PolicyPreview.ruleAt()`): *Very strict: aims under 2.0%, at 1.0% · on target it sets 4.00% · at this inflation …*; and the rule's reason on the card says what the step aims at once it is off Standard. `CentralBankCheck`'s probe city, the playtest's founding in its seed 5's shape to month 600 and then 240 months with nothing built, ran at 2.04% a year very strict, 2.23% at Standard and 3.29% very loose, the dial at most 5.38%, 4.34% and 11.74%, and trust 0.95, 0.95 and 0.82 on average. Over the same branch and horizon seeds 2, 3 and 4 held the same order; seed 1's loose end ran 0.06 points under Standard, and seed 0, a shrinking city with over a fifth of its workers out of work, ran both ends the other way. Played instead from the founding, 480 months, a boom swamps the dial — very strict's peaked at 56.7% against Standard's 38.0% and very loose's 24.9% — and all three came back down without reaching the stop. It is saved by name under its own key, an older save reads Standard, and moving it is a decision on the central bank's record.

### Advances, the ceiling, and who is paid

A treasury below zero at the top of the month is advanced its gap at the policy rate, repays from the first cash above zero before anything else, and may owe up to a ceiling in months of its trailing revenue. The emergency note it used to sell its bank is retired, and a save still carrying one runs it off. The ceiling is a dial since 0.7.2 — `advancesCeilingMonths`, 0 to `MAX_ADVANCES_CEILING` 36, default `DEFAULT_ADVANCES_MONTHS` 6, chips at 3, 6, 12, 24 and 36 months on the monetary page — saved under its own key, so an older save reads six, and held in a playtest by `-Dplaytest.advancesMonths`.

Past the ceiling the treasury pays by Jerus's rule, asked what a treasury past its ceiling does: *"pay promises first, cut the rest."* Every payment goes through `Game.treasuryPays(TreasuryLine, amount)`. **Promises** — pensions, EI, health, the schools, the police and prisons, the city's own services, coupons and principal at home and abroad, the interest on the advances, the student loans already lent — are paid whatever it takes, past the ceiling if they must. **Discretionary** lines — the subsidies, the students' grants, repairs to the city's own buildings — are paid only from cash at or above zero once the ceiling has bound, and what they are refused is owed as interest-free **arrears**, by line — rows of the Government Overview's CENTRAL BANK card since 0.7.31 — and paid down first when cash returns. **Purchases** — land, buildings, capital into the bank, reserves, buybacks — are simply not made. The central bank's profit — the interest it takes on its advances and, since 0.7.1, on the paper it holds, less what reserves cost it — is remitted to the treasury the next month as a revenue line; a loss is carried and recovered before anything is remitted again.

It is the floor the overdraft never had. On 0.7.0, held at a 10% dial, the six seeds that had compounded to $193 quadrillion and NaN ended owing $0.1–2.0B, the audit closed every month, and seed 0's bank failures went from 161 to 16; the arrears grew in a straight line rather than compounding, and none of the five that drew recovered. On 0.7.2, with the currency answering the real rate, none of the six draws at all. The default seed on 22 September never drew an advance: it ended owing nothing against a ceiling of $2.71B, six months of its revenue; nor did it on 28 September, against a ceiling of $3.20B, nor on 1 October, against $2.94B, nor on 5 October, at 0.7.49, against $3.63T.

**Since 0.7.15 a city can run on them from its first month.** Asked whether an Insane city should play before it borrows, Jerus chose *"Play runs on advances"*, and the refusal 0.7.14 had put on the play clock is gone. An Insane city that never borrows pays its land bond's dollar coupon and its founders' pensions in month one from nothing, ends it $6.47k overdrawn, and is advanced the gap at the next settle; its discretionary lines are refused, because a ceiling of no revenue leaves no room, and its private sector pays tax from month two, so a year on its treasury holds $7.1M. The time skip no longer stops at an empty treasury either (*"Skip runs too"*); it says what the central bank advanced. A failed bank's resolution is paid through the same door since 0.7.14, the advances taking whatever the treasury's cash does not ([the bank](#14-the-bank)).

### The holdings dial: QE and QT

Quantity, beside the price. `CentralBank.targetShare` is the share of the city's outstanding *term* paper — serials and term loans, not notes — the central bank aims to hold, from nothing to `MAX_QE_SHARE` — half until 0.7.15, because past half the market it is the market, and all of it since, as a backstop (below); chips every ten points on the monetary page, saved, and held in a playtest by `-Dplaytest.qeShare`. Once a month, in `openMarketOperation()` — after the treasury has settled with its central bank and before the market is priced, so this month's quotes carry it — the holding moves toward the dial by at most `QE_SPEED`, a quarter, of the largest of the dial, the setting before it and the share actually held: four months at most, exactly four to or from nothing, so a sale finishes where a share of the gap never would. It never buys at issue, bar its own maturing par since 0.7.15, and it trades only paper that has already been paid for, pro rata, at the curve's market value — the bank's first, and since 0.7.15 the households' after it; buying is money issued and selling money retired; it carries the paper at face and takes what it paid above or below face into the month's profit, so the remittance carries it. The coupons on its share are destroyed and come back as the remittance: *debt to itself*. The setting before the dial is saved beside it and restored without moving (`restoreTargetShare()`), because the first build forgot the pace on every reload.

```
compression(months) = termPremium(months) × min(1, share of the term paper held / FULL_COMPRESSION_SHARE) × QE_COMPRESSION     // FULL_COMPRESSION_SHARE .5 · QE_COMPRESSION 1.0
```

So at 30% held the fifty-year sits exactly 0.90 points under the table and the note has not moved, and at half the term premium is gone. With the playtest's borrowing sent home and the dial at 30% (0.7.1), the central bank bought exactly 30% of each issue's face in four months from the month after its settle, at 0.99 to 1.05 of face, and took 0.90 points off the fifty-year while it held it. It moved nothing else — the runs match the ones without it month for month until the first purchase and drift apart after, trajectory noise rather than a channel — because the playtest's advisor reads only the short end, which the compression never touches. `CentralBankCheck` sections 11–15 assert the purchase at `QE_SPEED` × 30% at face and at the market value, M0 moved by exactly it, `compression(240)` exact and the note untouched, the coupon destroyed and remitted, the dial to nothing selling back within the speed's months, the pace across a save, and a reform that scales the holdings and not the dial.

**The backstop.** Jerus: *"central bank bond holding can ve 100% if one wants"* — *"for when banks and investors dont want government bonds, its also f bank is in dire state, to not harm it further"*. Since 0.7.15 the dial runs to the whole of the term paper (`MAX_QE_SHARE` 1.0). It buys the bank's paper first and then the households', at the curve's value, through the door a household short of money sells by; the compression stays whole from half, with nothing more past it (`FULL_COMPRESSION_SHARE`); and the city's floor is split by who holds the paper, so that the more of it the central bank holds, the less the bank's state reaches the city's rate ([the city's borrowing](#13-the-citys-borrowing)). And it **rolls what it holds**: 0.7.15's first build found that when a piece it held fell due, the rollover sold the replacement to the bank, which funded it at the window and failed, so on Jerus's word, *"Build the rollover fix"*, it takes its maturing par again at issue as a non-competitive add-on at the issue's price, par for par, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's practice; past its dial it lets what it holds run off, as the Fed did under QT; and at 100% it takes the whole issue when the market's part is nothing (*"Yes, the backstop"*), which the Fed never does. And last year's surplus pays the market's part of what falls due first and then the central bank's par (*"Surplus pays everyone"*), so a city in surplus clears its paper whoever holds it; when a surplus pays only part of the par, the paper shrinks under the central bank and it ends that month over its dial, and the holdings step sells the excess to the bank — Jerus: *"Leave it (as built)"*.

The default city never owes paper at home, so the dial cannot be measured on it: its runs, and the autopilot's, are 0.7.14's to the byte. Where the dial bites, on eight seeds a setup: a Lean founding at 50% failed its bank 12 times and ended at 159,372 people on average, and at 100% 11 times and 156,877, paying all its paper off again between months 252 and 1,080 with the central bank rolling in only 10 months across the eight; held at 25%, where the spiral is, the city ended at 4,529 people with the dial at nothing, 5,626 at 50% and 1,047 at 100%, with 43, 105 and 61 failures. That first build's better 25% city at 100% — 9,476 people — was a loop: each rollover sold the bank about three times the maturing face for cash, and the central bank bought it back under face and remitted the gain. Par for par ended it. At 100% the central bank is the buyer when nobody else is; it does not limit what the city can sell. A 0.7.15 save with the dial past half, opened in 0.7.14, loads at half, and Jerus left it so. `CentralBankCheck`'s sections 17 to 20 assert the whole of the paper with the compression whole from half, the floor split by holder, the par taken again at issue, and the surplus paying the market's part first.

### The defence spends

Until 0.7.2 the vault damped a push on the currency and not a dollar left it: a capacity that cost nothing, which is why the default player never saw it work. Now the central bank **sells**. On a month the currency is pushed weaker and the city ran a deficit, it sells the vault's capacity times the month's own deficit — its current plus financial account when negative, in dollars at the month's rate, not the trailing window the push reads — and never more than the vault holds. What damps the push is the **realised** absorption, what was sold over what was wanted, so a full vault damps what its cover says, one running low damps less each month, and an empty one damps nothing. A push with no deficit that month sells and damps nothing; a rise is never met, because leaning against appreciation is buying dollars, which is a decision, not something a vault does by standing there.

```
push        = trade pressure + ratePressure        // ratePressure = −(realRateDifferential + EXPECTED_REVERSION × ln(rate / parity)) × RATE_PULL, held within MAX_RATE_PRESSURE either way; the reversion since 0.7.42
absorption  = MAX_ABSORPTION × min(1, cover / COMFORTABLE_COVER)      // .85 at six months of imports
dollarsSold = min(absorption × deficitUsd, vault)          // only on a push to weaken, in a month that ran a deficit
realised    = dollarsSold / deficitUsd
rate        ×= 1 + push × (1 − realised) × openness × DRIFT_SPEED
rate        ×= ((1 + credibility × target) / (1 + world inflation))^1/12    // the anchored drift, since 0.7.42: see the currency
rate        += (parity − rate) × REVERSION
```

**A capital transaction, not money destroyed.** The buyer is the world, and the local money it hands back is money the pools had already paid out for the imports: the deposit half of the textbook happened the day the goods were bought. So the vault falls by the dollars, the central bank's equity falls by their local price (`vaultSpent()`, a line under equity on the Money page, *spent defending the currency since founding*), M0 does not move, no pool moves and the audit declares nothing, and the month's profit and the remittance are untouched. It is booked at the reprice, after the audit, through `dollarsSold()`, with the month and the lifetime kept apart (`getDefendedThisMonth()`, `getDefendedLifetime()`). The first build retired the money instead and took seed 0's M0 to minus $255M, a bank that had destroyed more than it ever made. Trade's reserves page says what was sold this month and since founding, and since 0.7.35 The currency page's WHAT IS MOVING IT draws the forces, the defence among them ([the currency](#16-prices-the-currency--the-world)).

**What it did with the founders' billion**, when a city was founded on one (0.7.2), was spend it on structural deficits, not crises. On the eight seeds every one sold more than half of it and six all but 1%, over 22 to 225 sale months, half of it gone by month 628 to 3,747 — while the playtest's advisor buys it back with the treasury's cash, so that one seed sold US\$1.29B out of a US\$1B vault. `MAX_ABSORPTION` .85 at a `COMFORTABLE_COVER` of six months spends about 0.85 months of cover per deficit-sized month, so a vault at six months of cover meets the first deficit-sized month at full strength and damps less every month after, about half as hard five months in. On the default seed on 22 September the defence sold US\$1.06B in 174 months, the most US\$62.3M in month 725; half the founders' dollars were gone by month 726 and all but a hundredth by month 1,774, the vault ended at US\$134k, and \$531M of the central bank's equity went on it. Since 0.7.10 a city is founded on US\$25M, not a billion ([founding a city](#17-founding-a-city)), and the default playtest's vault was half gone by month 141 against 739 and empty by month 374 against 987, the defence spending US\$202M against US\$1,189M, while the worst currency month fell from 3.34 to 1.54 local to the dollar (0.7.10). On 28 September the defence sold US\$24.9M in 63 months, the most US\$3.7M in month 66; the vault was at its lowest, US\$973k, in month 973, half the founders' dollars were gone by month 753, \$17.3M of the central bank's equity went on it, and the advisor's purchases left US\$53.1M in the vault at the end. On 1 October it sold US\$39.2M in 114 months, the most US\$9.0M in month 3,447; the vault was at its lowest, US\$2k, in month 132, half the founders' dollars were gone by month 40 and all but a hundredth by month 51, \$31.7M of the central bank's equity went on it, and the vault ended at US\$33.0M. On 5 October, at 0.7.49, it sold US\$475.3M in 74 months, the most US\$68.3M in month 2,121; the vault was empty in month 273, half the founders' dollars were gone by month 38 and all but a hundredth by month 49, \$24.3B of the central bank's equity went on it, and the vault ended at US\$489.8M. Whether the defence should answer only a crisis is Jerus's.

### The demand channel

For the rate to bite at home a household's saving has to answer the real return, and since 0.7.3 it does. What a household spends above a basket a head is scaled by one factor a month, struck on the **real deposit rate** — the bank's deposit rate less the inflation savers expect, `Game.realDepositRate()`, and less the year's inflation until 0.7.42 — before the households plan. Deposits and not the curve, because the marginal saver's return is what the bank pays on every balance every month. Subsistence never moves; the propensity's share, the wealth term and the surplus the counter and the table spend out of all scale by it, so a hike does not hand what the grocer lost to the counter — scaling the want alone had pushed the surplus *up*, and a hike raised spending. At a factor of one every line is the old plan to the bit. Nothing is saved; the load path strikes it again. The monetary page says it in words: *"savers earn X% real, so households spend Y% of what they would at zero."* Since 0.7.47 its preview of a dial not yet applied reads the same expected inflation (`PolicyPreview.realDepositRateAt()`), where it had gone on subtracting the year's: in the 2,400-month city it previewed −3.28% at the dial in force against the month's −1.705%, and previews −1.699% now.

```
spendFactor     = clamp(1 − SAVING_RESPONSE × realDepositRate, SPEND_FLOOR, SPEND_CEILING)
realDepositRate = the bank's deposit rate − expected inflation     // the year's inflation until 0.7.42
// SAVING_RESPONSE 1.0, provisional, Jerus's number · SPEND_FLOOR 0.5 · SPEND_CEILING 1.5
```

So the chain runs from the dial, to the deposit rate the bank chooses as a share of it (until 0.7.7, a share of what its book and its reserves earned), to the real deposit rate, to the factor, to the plan, to the shelf, which since 0.7.43 clears on what the plan will spend. `MonetaryCheck` section 6 — the assertion that had waited since the first batch — holds one founding at 3, 10, 20 and 40% from month 25 to 60 and asserts that **inflation falls with the rate**: each row no higher than the one before within `MEASUREMENT_NOISE`, and the 3% row at least `TRANSMISSION_FLOOR`, a point a year, above the 40% row. The noise was 0.05 points a year until 0.7.11, when a ten-year fixed mortgage that locks in the month it is written put the rows held a month late up to 0.053 apart, and on Jerus's word it is 0.10; on 28 September they differ by 0.000 to 0.035, on 1 October by 0.000 to 0.066, and on 5 October by 0.000 to 0.056. 0.7.42 alone put them 0.165 apart and was left red against the 0.100; 0.7.43's shelf brought them back under it on the model's own change. It went green at 1.032 points on 0.7.3, where 0.7.2 read 0.996 and would have failed, read 1.428 on 0.7.7, and read 1.304 points on 28 September. Since then its founding has been made to build a hospital through the window, so that its builders keep their crews (0.7.17), and to put up its bakery, diner and boutique (0.7.18), and on 1 October it reads **4.960 points**, with the city at a 3% dial inflating 3.82% a year: a different town from the one 28 September measured, so the two readings are two towns, not a trend. On 5 October, at 0.7.49, on the same town, it reads **8.209 points**: at a 3% dial it inflates 6.16% a year and at 40% it deflates 2.05%, and the dear dial's real deposit rate is +4.59% against −3.48% at the cheap one. The anchor and a shelf that clears on money are what moved it (below).

> **The channel was in, and until 0.7.42 it moved very little**
>
> Most of that point was the currency's: the rate moved inflation by making the currency dearer and imports cheaper, which it did before the channel existed. The channel fired every month and reached almost nothing, for four reasons. **Weak pass-through.** Until 0.7.7 the bank paid savers `DEPOSIT_PASS_THROUGH`, 45%, of what it *earned*, not a rate, so the deposit rate carried about a quarter of the dial — 11% at a 40% dial — and the factor ran only from 0.99 to 0.88 across the whole range. Since 0.7.7 the bank passes on a share of the dial it chooses, and on 28 September the same founding's deposit rate ran from nothing at a 3% dial to 13.21% at 40%, and the factor from 1.000 to 0.858; on 1 October the re-caused founding's ran from nothing to 6.52%, and the factor from 1.083 to 0.930. **Nothing to act on in the index.** Food was four fifths of it, and the shelf did not answer money at the margin: at the founding it sits at its floor on every row, and in a grown city the want is thirty times what the shops can serve, so the scarcity mark-up reads the shops' coverage and a tenth less want moves no price. **The counter and the table were not in the index**, and that is where discretionary money goes. **Saved money compounds:** at a held high rate savings earn interest paid in new money, and the wealth term spends a fixed share of a stock growing faster than the factor cuts it. On 0.7.3's default eight the factor's median was 0.994; held at 10, 30 and 50% the six broke seeds swung 1.25×, 1.75× and 2.24× where they had swung 1.24×, 1.90× and 2.01×, and their index ended *higher* at 30 and 50%. A held high rate does not deflate through demand.
>
> *A demand channel needs a price that answers to demand.* The assertion was green on the transmission as a whole, not on this channel, and the box said the next rate that bit would be a shelf priced by scarcity against money rather than coverage. That is what 0.7.43 built, on the anchor 0.7.42 laid (below): the shelf clears on what the households would spend at each price, the index has five parts with the counter and the table in it, and a held high rate no longer feeds the savers' trap — on sixteen seeds a dial held at 15% lowers inflation by 2.85 points against its twin, where on 0.7.41 it raised it.

### The anchor: what people expect

Jerus: *"even if you set central bank to hold 100% of bonds, and set target inflation at 20%, and set the rates at 0% forever, other than at the beginning, you barely get any inflation, is it cause of the type of inflation?"* It was. Until 0.7.41 the model made only cost-push inflation — import prices through the rate, and wages chasing the index into rent — and every push ended as a one-off level step, pulled back by money constants fixed in founding money: the shelf's opening price, the price of ground, the cash in every building's cost, the fees. No price in the index read money, spending or wealth; with a 20% target the rule sat at the 0% floor until inflation passed 18%; and under the autopilot a city ran at about 0% a year whatever the dial said. A real economy's anchor is not a constant. It is what people expect, and what they expect depends on whether they believe the bank. Four versions answered it, 0.7.42 to 0.7.45, each built by a fresh implementer on a design that was measured before it was fixed.

**Expected inflation** (`Expectations`, 0.7.42) is the target weighted by the bank's **credibility** plus recent inflation weighted by the rest, never under minus one per cent (`EXPECTED_FLOOR`), recent inflation being the year's rate smoothed a twelfth of the way a month (`ADAPT_MONTHS`). Credibility runs from a quarter to 0.95, and a new city, like a save from before the anchor, starts believing the bank at 0.80 (`KMIN`, `KMAX`, `KSEED`). It is hard to win and slow to lose while the bank fights. With smoothed inflation within a point of the target (`TOLERANCE`) it climbs a sixtieth of the way to 0.95 a month, about five years to most of it (`GAIN_MONTHS`); off target it falls toward a quarter at up to a twenty-fourth of the way a month (`LOSS_MONTHS`), in proportion to the miss past the point, full at four points more (`MISS_SCALE`), and only as far as the bank is not leaning against it: a dial at the rule's advice, or past it, keeps every bit of credibility a supply shock would otherwise cost — since 0.7.52 the Standard rule's advice, however strict the bank, so a looser bank loses trust as far as it falls short of it. A floor of a tenth, lost to shocks whatever the rate, was measured to lock the founding at 10% a year. The **expected price level** compounds at expected inflation from 1.0 in the month the basket is based; before that everyone expects the target, the level is founding's and credibility waits. The level is drift-only: a save from before 0.7.42 seeds it at 1.0, because its constants are still in founding money, and a catch-up to the index was measured to be a unit root with the floor.

```
smoothed     += (inflation − smoothed) / ADAPT_MONTHS                       // 12
credibility  += (KMAX − credibility) / GAIN_MONTHS                       // on target: smoothed within TOLERANCE, a point
credibility  −= (credibility − KMIN) / LOSS_MONTHS × min(1, (miss − TOLERANCE) / MISS_SCALE) × (1 − lean)
expected     = max(EXPECTED_FLOOR, credibility × target + (1 − credibility) × smoothed)
level        ×= (1 + expected)^1/12                                   // from 1.0 when the basket is based
```

**What follows it.** Every money constant that prices something is struck at the expected level at the top of each month, never at the index, so that no constant reads a price it sets (`Game.restrikeMoneyConstants()`): the shelf's opening price, the price of ground, every template's cash cost and upkeep, the care and burial fees, the tuition table, the pension's wage base, a founding share's par, the bank's paid-in capital and its account fee, and the fare; and what `Game` strikes for itself — the fixed grant, the new-home rebates and the issue fee — reads the same level. The numerical guards and grains follow the currency's unit alone, and anything priced in world money is the world's. Wages take half their indexing from expected inflation and half from chasing the index ([labour](#11-labour--schools)). The real rates are ex ante, the rate less *expected* inflation: the differential the currency reads, the deposit rate the households save on, the investors' hurdle and, since 0.7.44, the landlords' lender ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)). The currency drifts at the credible part of the target, and investors expect a currency away from parity to come back ([the currency](#16-prices-the-currency--the-world)). And since 0.7.43 every sticky seller's price drifts at expected inflation: the shelf, the two rents and the kitchens' and the boutiques' margins.

**The shelf answers money** since 0.7.43, which is the demand channel's missing half. Groceries are asked for at a price, at most a basket a head, inelastic, wanted whole up to half again over the floor and capped by the household's money; the shops' price moves a sixth of the way a month, in logs, toward the price that clears that demand against what their coverage lets them hand over, between a floor and a cap half again over it ([goods and markets](#7-goods--markets)); and the index has five parts, the meals and the luxuries where discretionary money goes among them ([the index](#16-prices-the-currency--the-world)). Hunger is counted in baskets, and a food assistance dial, nothing by default, pays vouchers to the households the shelf would price out ([promises](#12-tax-policy--gdp)).

**What it did**, measured on sixteen seeds under five policies, against a score written as code before the first number was seen. Under the autopilot at 2%, inflation from month 240 ran at 0.05% a year on 0.7.41, no seed of the sixteen within a point of the target, and at 2.28% on 0.7.44, from 2.02% to 2.40%, all sixteen within it; 0.7.49's sixteen ran at 2.22%. One import shock, the world's prices up 30% at month 600, is a level step that settles: 12.36% over its twin at the peak, and in its second decade 2.87% a year, 0.41 points over its twin. A dial held at 15% from month 600 now lowers inflation, by 2.85 points against its twin, at a cost of 2.25 points of unemployment, where on 0.7.41 it fed the savers' interest trap and raised it. Every seed took off, earlier than before, and the money audit closed in every month of every run. Three criteria still fail, each for a reason that was measured. A 0% dial held from month 600 in a city meant to be slack ran at 7.07% a year, because the city at month 600 was taking off; held from month 1,800, measured on 0.7.43, it ran at 3.16%. A 0% dial held in a hot young city gives a persistent burst and never an accelerating rate, because the wage curve has no growth term and credibility floors at a quarter. And a boom can still hold year-on-year inflation over 10% for 12 or 13 months, against a limit under 12, as a shelf runs from its floor to its cap. All three are Jerus's to confirm ([open questions](#25-open-questions)).

**On the screen** since 0.7.45, the header's INFLATION tile reads *expect x% · trust 80%* under the rate, *exp x% · 80%* where it is tight, and NEEDS YOU has a PRICES row, amber in a month credibility fell and red when it fell under half (`CityNeeds.TRUST_RED`), its reading the miss and how far the dial sits from the rule's advice — the Standard rule's, and named so off Standard, since 0.7.52; the row reads the move, not the level, so that it does not stay red through the recovery a player buys by leaning against the miss. Policy › Money draws THE ANCHOR beside THE CURRENCY'S DRIFT, and the hub flags *Trust is falling*. City History keeps expected inflation, credibility and the expected level among the 23 series 0.7.45 added. `ExpectationsCheck` holds the anchor in nine sections: before the basket is based; credibility won at `GAIN_MONTHS` on target; a miss nobody leans against costing it and a lean keeping it; the floor; the level compounding at expected inflation; the wages half and half; the money constants at the expected level; the currency's level for a real gap and its anchored drift; and the anchor through a save and a save from before it.

The chapter's harnesses are `CentralBankCheck` (twenty-one sections: the identity, the floor, the window, the note's price, advances and the ceiling, the arrears rule, the autopilot, the save and a reform, the holdings dial and the ceiling dial, and since 0.7.15 the whole of the paper, the floor split by holder, the par taken again at issue and the surplus paying everyone, and since 0.7.52 how strictly the rule holds the target), `HoldersCheck`, `CurrencyCheck`, `MonetaryCheck` section 6, `CreditCheck` section 11, `TreasuryCheck`, and since 0.7.42 to 0.7.44 `ExpectationsCheck`, `GroceryCheck` and `SupplierCreditCheck`, and they are listed in [how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked). The central bank's month is not saved, so after a reload the Money page's *this month* lines read nothing until the month turns; that is on the list too.

## 16. Prices, the currency & the world

*The city has a price level of five parts, chained every ten years, a currency with a name that drifts at what the city believes of its bank, a vault of dollars, a balance of payments, hot money that comes for the spread, a rent market that no longer follows wages, and — since the surplus had nowhere to go — somewhere for its savings to sit.*

### A price index, and prices that ration

A fixed basket, priced every month, is the city's price level, and it does not re-weight to hide inflation. Until 0.7.43 it was the shelf price and rent, weighted by what households spent in a base month two years after the city started shopping, and fixed for good. **Since 0.7.43 it has five parts** (`PriceIndex`): groceries, rent, meals, luxuries and the services, the services being a fee index of its own over the care fees, tuition, the fare and the bank's account fee, each weighed as its fees were paid. The weights are what the households spent over the trailing twelve months (`WEIGHT_MONTHS`), luxury held to 15% of the basket and its excess spread over the rest pro rata (`LUXURY_WEIGHT_CAP`) — uncapped it would have been 63% in the 2,400-month city — and a part nobody bought holds its last price. Every 120 months (`REBASE_MONTHS`) the basket is struck again on the year before and **chained** to the old one at the level it reached, so the level runs on unbroken and a year's rate runs through the link; a one-month rebase was measured to give food a weight of nothing in a crash month. A save from before 0.7.43 waits for its first month to link its basket, at the level its own old basket strikes. The basket is first fixed only after 24 months of real shopping with both food and rent in it (`PriceIndex.SETTLING_MONTHS`), about month 37 in a Standard city, because a city based earlier had a basket that was 96% rent and never saw food prices; and the first year-on-year rate comes a year of readings after that, about month 50. Until then every screen and the central bank read inflation as zero. The play-through of 0.7.19 read the price card's *no year yet* at month 13 as a bug; since 0.7.20 it counts down, *rate in ~37 mo*, a floor while the basket is not fixed and exact once it is, and Jerus chose to *"Keep the countdown"* over fixing the basket sooner or adding a provisional reading. The shelf price was cost-plus and rose to 1.6× at total shortage until 0.7.43; since then it is a floor and a clearing price half again over it at most, moving a sixth of the way a month in logs, so a short city spends more at the shops for fewer goods by what its households would pay rather than by a count of heads ([goods and markets](#7-goods--markets)), and People's WHO GOES SHORT, AND WHY says who went short and whether for money or for stock.

**The index remembers its own high and low water-marks**, and the month each was set. An end-of-run figure says where a city finished, not what it lived through: a run that ends at 0.98 having been at 1.31 and 0.62 is not the same city as one that never moved, and until the marks were kept there was no way to tell them apart from the outside. The pair and the swing between them are carried in the save; a city saved before the marks existed opens with both sitting on today's level, which is the only honest thing to say about a past nobody recorded.

**Rent is two markets**: family homes and studios, each with a cost floor from the cheapest template *that serves that segment*, at today's cash and materials prices spread over a landlord's yield of 5.8%, times that segment's households per front door, unbounded both ways, closing a twelfth of the gap a month because a lease is twelve months — in logs since 0.7.43, and drifting at expected inflation as it goes, so a landlord who expects prices to rise writes the next lease dearer with the market standing still (`Retail.stickyPrice()`, the one form every seller in the city prices by). Taking one floor across the whole portfolio and applying it to both legs was what turned rent into a constant — every building earning the same $445 a head whatever it cost, and a city that built 138 low-rise blocks and no studios with 1,847 households wanting one. Struck per segment, studio rent went $445 to $706 and studio doors over 4,000 months went from zero to 19,920. Land is deliberately *not* in the floor: land price is a capitalised rent, an output of this market, and feeding it back in grew a number because it grew. Overbuild and rent falls below cost and the landlords eat it.

### The city's dollar, and what moves it

The local currency was the **Danzik dollar, D\$**, until 0.7.10, and since then it is the city's own: named after the city by default — a city founded as Arden pays in the Arden dollar, A\$, ARD — or by hand, with a three-letter code that is never USD, and a save from before loads as Danzik, in the Danzik dollar, D\$, DZD. This page writes D\$ for it, against the US dollar. Since 0.7.2 its rate moves on three things: pressure from the balance of payments; the **real** rate differential, `Game.realRateDifferential()` — the policy rate less the inflation the city expects, its year's inflation until 0.7.42, against the world's base rate less the world's realised inflation — at `RATE_PULL` 4 a point, so money moves toward the higher real return; and a pull toward relative parity (`REVERSION`, a fifteen-year half-life) that says where the rate should end up. The drift that moved it every month by the whole of the inflation differential, `rate *= 1 + (local − world) / 12`, is **deleted**. With imports repricing through the rate, wages chasing the whole index and the shelf cost-plus, a gain of one on that link meant a city whose prices rose 40% a year saw its currency fall 40% a year by rule, whatever its central bank did; Jerus's 0.6.9 city, 399× its founding prices in twenty-five years, was that loop run for 306 months. The inflation differential still reaches the currency, through parity, which rises with local prices, and through the trade balance a cheap or dear currency earns — but not month by month, by rule. **A spiral needs an actual outflow to continue, and a credible real rate stops it:** in `CurrencyCheck`, ten months of 40% inflation with the real gap at nothing move the rate to 1.0067, the parity pull alone, where the drift would have taken it to 1.3649. The world has its own inflation, a persistent moving average drawn low in 1–8%, deterministic, with its level pulled back to trend so that 333-year runs stay usable.

**Since 0.7.42 a drift is back, in the one form with no inflation in it**: every month the rate moves by the credible part of the city's target against the world's realised inflation, (1 + credibility × target) / (1 + world inflation) a year (`Game.anchoredDrift()`), and by nothing before the basket is based ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)). And investors **expect a currency away from parity to come back**, at 0.15 of the log gap a year (`ForeignAccounts.EXPECTED_REVERSION`): the rate's pressure is the real gap less what a strong currency is expected to give back, so a sustained real gap moves the currency to a level, e^−gap/0.15 of parity (`uipLevel()`), a three-point gap 22% from it, rather than a drift for as long as the gap lasts. Both were measured before they were fixed: with the expected inflation in the real rate, a 0% dial under a 2% expectation is a two-point negative gap for good, and without the reversion it compounded into a currency falling every month; with no drift at all the currency ended at 0.43 to 0.46 of parity and growth halved; and a drift at the whole of expected inflation ran at 41–66% a year with the dial held at 0%. The reversion also bounds what new money leaks abroad.

```
current account   exports − imports − interest paid abroad − foreign savers' interest
financial account what the city's owners send abroad, less what comes home
position          reserves − foreign debt   // revaluation lives here, not on any statement
real rate gap     (policy − expected inflation) − (world base − world inflation)   // RATE_PULL 4 a point; the city's year's inflation until 0.7.42
its pressure      −(real rate gap + EXPECTED_REVERSION × ln(rate / parity)) × RATE_PULL
anchored drift    (1 + credibility × target) / (1 + world inflation) − 1, a year
hot money         spread = max(depositRate, cityRate) − worldRate − countryPremium   // at most MAX_SPREAD
```

The caps on the channel are numerical guards now: `MAX_RATE_PRESSURE` went from .8 to 4.0 and binds only at a hundred-point real gap, and the hot money's appetite, `CapitalFlows.MAX_SPREAD`, from .06 to .25, measured, until 0.7.7 took the strain premium out of every rate, against the city's rate net of it (`getRateBeforeStrain()`, gone with it), because what a strained bank charges is not a return. `RATE_PULL` went from 6 to 4, the one retune the batch allowed itself: at six the loop's gain was 1.44 against the deleted drift's 1.0, and one seed whose dial sat at 0.08% went to the guard with its prices at 115× founding; at four the gain is 0.96, and no default seed goes near a guard. The cost is that a credible real rate buys two thirds of the support it did. *The channel is only as good as the hand on the dial.* Since 0.7.35 Trade's currency page draws the forces as the model previews them, WHAT IS MOVING IT, NEXT MONTH: THE PRESSURE as bars either side of a line, stronger to the left — the trade term, the real rate and the two together — with the vault's defence and the openness under it (*trade ≥ output (100%)* when the model's clamp holds), and WHICH COMES TO, the month's push, the anchored drift since 0.7.45 and the pull back to parity, adding to next month's move exactly (`ForeignAccounts.previewPush()`, `previewDrift()`, `previewPull()`, `previewMove()`; `ForeignCheck` asserts the sum to 1e-12), in the money blues and never a verdict's colour, with where the real rate alone would hold the rate and what the anchor hands it beside them. What the reprice was handed rides the foreign accounts' saved array, the defence at slots 25–27 and the real differential with its two inflations at 28–30, so the page survives a reload.

**And since 0.7.3 there is no guard a player will meet.** `ForeignAccounts.MAX_RATE` and `MIN_RATE` were 100 and .01 and pinned the currency — the last acts of Jerus's year book were a currency at its guard with imports no longer rising — and they are 1e9 and 1e-9 now, scaled by a reform: a guard against a rate run to nothing or to infinity, never a price the game expects to see. Past a hundredth of a cent the rate turns round and says what a US cent costs — the strip's second line did, and since 0.7.21 the RATE tile's (i) does — *US¢1 = D$1,000* at a rate of 100,000, instead of printing 0.00¢, and every page prints a rate through one formatter (`Money.fxRate()`). On the default seed on 22 September its dearest dollar was 1.000 local, in month 2; it spent no month weaker than twice parity and none at a guard, prices averaged +0.05% a year, and the run ended with the rate at 0.482 local to the dollar, 53% under a parity of 1.016. On 28 September its dearest dollar was again 1.000 local in month 2, with no month weaker than twice parity and none at a guard; prices averaged +0.04% a year, and the rate ended at 0.632, 37% under a parity of 1.006. On 1 October its dearest dollar was 1.428 local, in month 137, with no month weaker than twice parity and none at a guard; prices averaged +0.02% a year, and the rate ended at 0.571, 39% under a parity of 0.929. On 5 October, at 0.7.49, with the anchor, its dearest dollar was 813.952 local, in month 3,985: the currency drifted with prices that rose 1,213-fold, spent no month weaker than twice parity and none at a guard, prices averaged +2.15% a year, and the rate ended at 806.260, 23% under a parity of 1,053.126.

### The vault

**The founders leave one.** Jerus: *"of the 3.5B you start with, 1B is in usd in the reserve, so you only see 2.5B start with"* — because 99% of players would never buy reserves. From 0.6.10 to 0.7.9 a new city opened with D\$2.5B in the treasury and US\$1B in the vault, and since 0.7.10 it opens with D\$100M and US\$25M, the IMF's old three months of imports for a town of eight to ten thousand ([founding a city](#17-founding-a-city)); the dollars are bought on day one at the opening rate and booked as the purchase they are (`Game.FOUNDING_CASH`, `FOUNDING_RESERVE_USD`), and Trade's reserves page says where they came from among WHAT ELSE MOVED THE VAULT: *the founders left US\$25M in it*. **It is kept in dollars.** Checking the founding reserve found it in the wrong currency: it was a local figure at the price paid, so a hundredfold fall turned a US\$1B vault into US\$10M and its import cover fell with it, while the dollar debt beside it was revalued every month. The stock is dollars now, its local value the dollars times the rate, cover no longer moves with the currency, and the month's move is a revaluation line, not cash and not an audit flow. The treasury still buys and sells reserves, and since 0.7.6 the land office can be paid straight out of the vault ([land](#18-land)); the central bank reads the vault as its asset and, since 0.7.2, spends it defending the currency ([the central bank](#15-the-central-bank)).

**The reserves page** is in 0.7.35's shape. WHOSE IT IS draws the vault as one bar with the dollar paper and the parked money eaten out of it, what is left *the city's own* (`Game.getOwnReserves()`), and the treasury's position, the vault less the paper, which was called the net position. HOW LONG IT WOULD LAST is months of imports on a band, red under three (`ForeignAccounts.THIN_COVER`, the model's constant since 0.7.35, where the world prices a currency for a crisis) and amber under six (`COMFORTABLE_COVER`), with what three and six months would need; since 0.7.38 one formatter says it on Trade, Finances and the drawer alike, *under 0.1 months* rather than 0.0, *over 10 years* from 120 months and *none* with an empty vault (`Money.coverMonths()`), and the drawer colours it on the same two lines. BUY OR SELL FOREIGN MONEY is on 0.7.34's action button in the money blue, *to 3 months* and *to 6 months* among its steps, with what it would do to the cover before the press.

**A reserve defends a currency; it does not hold one down.** Jerus's rule, chosen from three after the founding reserve caused the very year book it was meant to prevent. The vault used to damp the pressure on the rate both ways, so a deep one muted the surplus a weak currency earns and the support of the policy rate — the two forces that pull a currency out of a spiral — and with the founders' dollars in it three of eight seeds reproduced Jerus's city, two of them past 140× their founding prices with the currency at its guard. It damps only a push weaker now, and the eight went to a median price swing of 1.60×, none past 2.81×, with sudden stops 8 to 0.

**And the header carries them.** From 0.6.10 to 0.7.20 a strip did, three panels between the population and the cash: prices against founding over inflation year on year; the rate both ways in the currency's own names, *US\$1 = D\$x* over *D\$1 = US¢y*, grey at or above parity and down to 5% under it, amber more than 5% below it and red past 25%; and since 0.7.4 *the price of money*, Jerus: *"on the top of the UI the bank rate, the central bank rate, both should be shown, as well as the rate you borrow in"* — three lines at the caption's weight, *central* the dial, *bank* the bank's lending rate on it, reading *no bank* or *failed* in red when the bank lends nothing, and *city* what the treasury borrows at. The inflation readout was grey within three points of the 2% target, amber outside it and red past 10% either way, and from 0.7.15 read from the player's target. Since 0.7.21 two of the header's tiles carry them, six tiles then and five since 0.7.24 ([the screen](#22-the-screen)). **INFLATION** reads the rate against the player's target, or *rate in ~N mo* before the first rate comes; it is green within three points of the target either side, amber further off, and red more than five points over it (`STRIP_INFLATION_OVER_TARGET`, Jerus: *"Red at target + 5 points"*) or with prices falling faster than 10% a year, whatever the target — so at the default target inflation of 7 to 10% reads red, where until 0.7.15 it read amber; and since 0.7.45 the line under it is the anchor, *expect 2.2% · trust 82%*, plain at rest, amber in a month trust fell and red when it fell under half, NEEDS YOU's PRICES row ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)). **RATE** shows the dial, with what a US dollar costs under it, and since 0.7.35 on the one parity rule the drawer's THE CURRENCY row and the Trade tab read too: grey within 25% of parity either side, amber from 25% and red from 50% (`ForeignAccounts.PARITY_WATCH`, `PARITY_FAR`, `parityLevel()`), grey when pinned. Until then it was grey near or above parity, amber more than 5% weaker and red past 25%, so a currency 25–50% stronger than parity turns it amber where it was grey, and 5–25% weaker reads grey where it read amber; the bank's prime and the city's rate are on its tooltip, and the three rates, the currency both ways and parity behind its (i). Every figure comes through a getter, and the header recomputes nothing.

### The surplus, and where it goes

A city that exports steel used to run a surplus of 30–50% of GDP with nowhere for it to go: no household bought anything abroad, nobody was paid a dividend, and no saver could own a foreign asset. The currency simply appreciated — about 10% a year, 1.20 down to 0.44 over 250 months — until every exporter in the city was dead, twenty times a run.

**Outward investment** is the door. A sector with an idle till buys the world's paper when the world pays more than the bank — forty times the spread, up to nine tenths of its wealth, moving 4% of the gap a month out and 10% home — and brings it home to fund a plan, pay a dividend or clear an overdraft. Households run the identical rule on their own savings. The coupon is *rolled where it is earned*, an income credit matched by a financial debit, so a rentier's surplus does not appreciate the currency, and the currency is priced on the whole balance rather than the trade half. The median run went from 33% below parity to 3.5%; exports went $33M to $124M a month. Since 0.7.12 a sector that owes nothing also puts a share of its wealth into the other sectors' bonds by the same rule, never its own, and still most of it goes abroad: after 0.7.12's eight default runs the companies held $6.7T abroad against $1.7T in their tills.

**And since 17 September the households spend abroad too**, through three doors the surplus did not have. A car the city did not make is an import at the ceiling; a watch always is, deliberately, so that wanting luxuries is money that leaves rather than going round again, and import substitution, if it ever comes, is something a player achieves; and every tonne the railway hauls burns fuel priced in the world's money, charged as a real import before there was any oil good, so that a reform could not forget it. A fourth door since 0.7.49: every journey a household drives to work burns $2.00 of fuel in the world's money at the rate (`Motoring.CAR_FUEL_PER_JOURNEY`), forty a month, an import Trade named as the households' fuel ([transport](#21-transport--vehicles)). Since 0.7.62 both are `FUEL`, a good the city can make: the drivers and the railway draw it off the refiners' tanks first and import the rest, so with no refinery the bill is what it was at the world's price level, and a refinery narrows the door by what it makes ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)); Trade lists fuel among its goods, the households and the railway among its buyers; since 0.7.76 the drivers' is petrol and the railway's diesel, both on fuel's band until the wholesale prices come, and the rest of a barrel is shipped. A meal is the exception — the food in it was already counted when it crossed the border, and the margin is wages and rent here.

**Hot money** comes for the spread net of the risk, at 8% of the gap a month, and leaves at 20%, straight into and out of the bank's deposits — which are its lending capacity, so the boom and the sudden stop are procyclical by construction. A run needs a *fragile* position (a material stock of it with under 25% backed by reserves) *and* a shock: the currency down 12% in a year, the bank insolvent, or a recent default. Always painful, never fatal.

Who owns the bank is a curve of financial deepening: a city with no savings has no domestic investors, a city with $124B on deposit owns its own banks. The bank's capital follows that curve. Its wholesale funding followed it too, which is what stopped a $156B book declaring its entire funding cost as interest paid abroad, until 0.7.0 moved the funding to the central bank's window, where the interest is paid at home and declared as money destroyed.

### The policy rate, and dropping zeros

The policy rate is the player's dial, with an advisory Taylor rule beside it saying what it would do and why, obeying the Taylor principle — and since 0.7.0 an autopilot that hands the rule the dial; the dial itself, and everything it now moves, is [the central bank](#15-the-central-bank). The playtest works the dial a quarter of the way toward the advice each time, because a rate that sat at 3% for three centuries would leave the whole monetary half untested. And once the city's own price index passes ten times founding, a **currency reform** unlocks: divide everything by 10, 100 or 1,000, the player's choice, never automatic. Every money constant in the game is an instance field seeded from its constant and redenominated with everything else, and since 0.7.42 struck every month as its founding figure over the unit times the expected price level, so a reform needs nothing new: the unit and the level are both in the product ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)). Foreign prices are the exception, quoted in someone else's money and reached through the rate. Since 0.7.47 a reform divides the month's transit bill and fares too, and since 0.7.49 the households' fuel; and the fare dial is read in founding money through the unit, so a reform no longer moves who rides, its cap being the founding cap in the new unit (`TaxPolicy.maxTransitFare()`) — in the 2,400-month city divided by a thousand, a month on, 41,394.6 riders and 11,077 households eligible for vouchers, the unreformed city's figures exactly, where they had read 43,627 and 49,778. The reform instant is bit-exact and conserves money; the following month is a few percent adrift in the discrete decisions, which is filed and has a plan.

## 17. Founding a city

*Until 0.7.10 every city was the same city at month zero: Danzik, founded on D\$2.5B and US\$1B, with no reason ever to borrow. A player founds a city now — its name, its money, what it starts with and the world's inflation — and the default start is small enough that the city borrows for what it builds.*

Jerus: *"lets reduce the cash the city starts with, both the foreign usd and the starting cash, what do you think makes sense? cause the city should borrow right"*. A trace of 0.7.9 found the treasury never going below D\$2.467B in thirty years: the young city spent \$0.1–2M a month and took in \$0.4–5M, owed nothing for about ninety years, and held a vault of 270 or more months of its imports. The endowment had been sized on 9 September to buy the opening, a coal power plant, and nothing since had asked it to do less. **Since 0.7.10 a city is founded on D\$100M and US\$25M**, Jerus's choice from the options put to him (`Game.FOUNDING_CASH`, `FOUNDING_RESERVE_USD`), sized so that the treasury could pay for the playtest's founding village and one of the first big works, and the city would borrow for the rest, the way towns pay for long-lived works, on bonds repaid over the asset's life — Britain's New Towns were built on sixty-year loans from the Exchequer, not on endowments. The vault follows the IMF's old rule of three months of imports. The endowment is still a game number, and the code says so.

**The village is the playtest's, not the player's.** The playtest places a founding village by hand before its advisor takes over — sixty houses, five shops, two farms and a depot — and the play-through of 0.7.19 found that a player's city gets none of it: after *Found the city* the treasury still held D\$100.0M, and month 3 had one house and thirteen people. A player's city starts with the treasury and the vault, and builds the rest. **The sticker is not the invoice.** What a new city pays for a building is the building and the material beyond its yard at the world's price, and since 0.7.19 the builders' sales tax on both: the water plant's D\$65.8M sticker was invoiced D\$109.6M and is D\$129.0M with the tax. So D\$100M pays for the village, D\$38.8M, and one of the wind farm, D\$36.5M, the school, D\$35.3M, or the police station, D\$52.9M; the option Jerus picked had been described on stickers, and he kept D\$100M once it was described on invoices, so the water plant is a bond from day one. That is why the build screen offers a twenty-year bond sized to the gap ([the city's borrowing](#13-the-citys-borrowing)): as 0.7.10 measured it, a Standard city a year on was D\$26.1M short of the water plant, issued D\$40.3M of face at 4.22%, raised D\$26.13M, paid about D\$56k a month, and had the plant in 57 months; on 1 October the same fixture was D\$58.3M short, issued D\$113.8M of face at 7.19%, raised D\$58.4M, paid D\$253k a month and had the plant in 137 months; and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, it was D\$61.8M short, issued D\$137.6M of face at 9.54% on a 3.45% coupon, raised D\$61.8M, paid D\$395k a month and had the plant in 146 months, with the audit closing every one (`NewGameCheck`, section 11). Since 0.7.42 every price on the page is struck at the price level the city expects, which at its founding is founding's, so the invoices a new city is quoted are the ones above.

### Found a city

Jerus, the same afternoon: *"a small thing at the start of the game where you choose the name of the city and the currency … and perhaps the settings to choose the starting cash and usd cash and offworld inflation rate … (with option to just start at default)"*. From 0.7.10 *Start New Game* opened **Found a city** (`ui/FoundingScreen`): the city's name; its money, named after the city or, with a tick, by hand, a name and three letters that are never USD; the money it is founded with; the world's inflation, moved there from Settings because it acts only at founding; and *Found with defaults*, which founded straight away. Each start showed what it would buy. Jerus, on the play-through: *"even the screen shouldnt say what the money could buy, the start screen should be real simple"*. Since 0.7.20 a start shows only what the founders leave, and since 0.7.21 *New city* on the main menu opens one panel over its dimmed skyline: the name, in a field that opens on *Danzik*; one line for its money, *"Its money: the Danzik dollar, D$ · name it yourself"*, where the link opens the name and its three letters in place; WHAT IT STARTS WITH, four cards, each its money in figures and one line on how hard it is, never what it buys, Standard marked *default*, and *Set your own amounts* for Custom; THE WORLD'S INFLATION, a row of five, with *"A faster world makes your money stronger. It can't be changed later."* and the rest behind an (i); and *Found the city* and *Back*. *Found with defaults* is gone, because the page opens on the defaults. None of 0.7.21's panel has been seen on a screen.

**Since 0.7.56 the panel founds a world as well.** THE WORLD, between the money and the inflation, is a seed: a whole number in a field in the figures' face, rolled when the page opens and again by a dice beside it, from 1 to 999,999,999, over *"The same number makes the same coast, lakes and ore."* Any whole number typed is a world; anything else keeps *Found the city* dark with *"Type the world as a whole number, like 4127, or roll the dice."* The defaults, the presets, the harnesses and the playtest found on world 4127 (`Founding.DEFAULT_WORLD_SEED`), so that they stay deterministic. What a seed makes is in [land](#18-land). The panel grew to about 710 pixels for it, under the 768-pixel window it is laid out for, and the row has not been seen on a screen either.

*The starts, in the order the page lists them (`Founding`)*

| Start | Treasury | Vault | What it is |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Insane | D$0 | US$0 | *"Nothing. The ground is owed on a 20-year bond."* Since 0.7.14: the ground it stands on owed abroad, a twenty-year dollar bond at 3% for US$2,100k |
| Lean | D$25M | US$10M | *"Tight. Borrow early."* Two-thirds of the playtest's village at a new city's invoices, three quarters until the builders' tax went into them; the city borrows from its first months |
| Standard | D$100M | US$25M | *"The usual start."* The default, sized on the playtest's village and one of the first big works at their invoices |
| Wealthy | D$2.5B | US$1B | *"Plenty to spare."* The start every city had from 0.6.10 to 0.7.9 |
| Custom | D\$6M–D\$10B | US\$0–US\$4B | for testing, not balanced for play; the floor was D$5M until 0.7.19, and is ten houses and a shop at a new city's invoices with the tax |

The choice is a record on the city (`Founding`), set once, saved under eight keys and since 0.7.56 a ninth, the world's seed, and never changed; the currency is a value per city, read through `game.getCurrency()`, because one process holds several cities — the harnesses', and the playtest's reloaded twin. The window's title and the save lists name the city, and every screen that prints its money names it. A save from before 0.7.10 loads as Danzik, in the Danzik dollar, founded on D\$2.5B and US\$1B, which is what it was; and one from before 0.7.56 is given a world made from its name, its founding treasury, its ground and its month (`Founding.derivedWorldSeed()`), the same at every load, which its next save keeps. A new game also founds on the autopilot and with the rollover on *same structure* since 0.7.13, with the bank's resolution automatic since 0.7.14, believing its central bank at 0.80 with prices expected at founding's since 0.7.42 ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)), and with its fund's withdrawal at one step, Norway's 3% a year, since 0.7.48; an older save keeps what it was played with, and one from before the anchor or the dial reads those two defaults. Building the screen found two bugs on the founding path: a new game after a load kept the loaded world's inflation, and a new city's first year was back-cast at the previous city's rate.

### Insane

Jerus: *"on game start, add a new difficulty called Insane, which is just you start with 0 cash, 0 vault, and a 20y bond 3% for the initial land cost … if easier the starting debt is abroad in usd"*. Since 0.7.14 it is the first start on the page: D\$0, US\$0, and a twenty-year dollar bond at 3% owed abroad for the starting land — 3,000,000 square feet at the land market's opening price of US\$0.70 a square foot, US\$2,100k — the figure, where since 0.7.67 a new city owns the 3,051,569 its whole blocks draw, which is on the list. No cash moves, because the founders' land was bought on it, and on the world's curve it is worth US\$375k on day 0. On day 0, as `FundCheck`'s section 12 prices it, a city with no revenue and no output pays the full spread: the founding card quoted the village's twenty-year bond at 13.90%, \$85,500k of face to raise \$32,978k, the six-month note at 13.00%, and the window abroad shut, until 0.7.20 took every figure off the founding screen. Since 0.7.21 Insane's card reads *nothing* for its money, and what is owed abroad for its ground is in its tooltip. 0.7.14 made the clock refuse to run until such a city had borrowed (Jerus: *"Borrow first"*); since 0.7.15 it runs on the central bank's advances from its first month instead ([the central bank](#15-the-central-bank)).

Of 0.7.14's eight Insane seeds, three became cities of 148,000, 206,000 and 148,000 people, and five spiralled on the city's own paper, ending with 3,686 to 10,118 people and \$420T to \$6,416T of it; the playtest's player borrows exactly the village's invoice, so every seed ran on the advances from month 3. Lean is hard too: D\$25M covered three quarters of the village then, and two-thirds since the tax went into the invoices; every seed borrows by month 4 to 14, and on 0.7.10 half of them ran out of cash around month 140 and lived on the advances for 450 to 500 months.

### What the smaller start did

As 0.7.10 measured it, making the founding a choice changed nothing else: founded Wealthy, the city reproduced three old ensembles byte for byte, all 24 seed-runs. The default playtest never borrows on D\$100M; its treasury bottoms out at D\$61–67M in its first two years and then grows. What the default run does show is the vault, half gone by month 141 against 739 and empty by month 374 against 987. Under the autopilot the bank failed 76 times against 49, and all of the rise was the vault's: D\$100M with the old US\$1B vault gave the old counts, and D\$2.5B with US\$25M the new ones, because without dollars to steady the currency a rule-held rate sees more imported inflation in the city's middle years. Held at 10%, every seed now runs dry in years 185 to 253, where three of eight did before: a city held at that rate loses money for centuries, and the D\$2.4B had been paying for it. And 42 fixtures in 25 harnesses had been living on the old treasury without saying so — ten went red and three were green only because they ran on a short calendar — and each funds itself explicitly now, with no premise and no tolerance moved.

## 18. Land

*A city stands on a world of its own: an Earth-sized square made from one number, its sea, coast and lakes and seven resources in finite fields, every one of them there to be seen. It starts with the dry ground of thirty of the old 100,000 sq ft blocks, drawn in whole 120 m blocks of that world, so that a power station and a water plant leave two spare — land is taught on turn one — and buys the rest a rectangle of whole blocks at a time, from six offers on each side that are never rerolled.*

### The world

Since 0.7.56 every city stands on a world of its own (`World`): a flat square the size of the Earth, 368 cells a side of 61.44 km, 511.2 million km² against the Earth's 510.1, with the city founded at its middle. It is made from one number, the seed chosen on the founding page ([founding a city](#17-founding-a-city)), and the same seed makes the same world on every machine: every value is a SplitMix64 hash of the seed and the place, and every sine and logarithm is `StrictMath`'s. It is measured in **plots** of 30 m, nested by powers of two — a tile is 32 plots, 0.96 km; a district 256, 7.68 km, which is what the map keeps (below); a cell 2,048 — and its ground is value noise in octaves: sea below a level each world finds for itself, so that 71% of it is sea, as the Earth's is; lakes on 3.7% of the land and forest on 31%, the measured shares of each (Verpoorter 2014; FAO 2020); and beaches at the shore. The founding site is the first point, spiralling out from the cells 25–75% land nearest the middle, that is dry at its centre and 600 m round, at least 60% land within 5 km, has the sea within 2.1 km but not within 1.35, and has an iron field within 2 km: a coast, with a lake beside it and a river that runs from a lake 64 to 90 plots away past the site to the sea. A world is built the first time it is asked for, in about half a second, and `WorldCheck` holds three of them to the design ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)). Two of the design's levels moved before it shipped: its percentiles had been taken at lattice points of every fine octave, where the noise is a bare lattice value, and made 5.0% of the land lakes and 24% forest, so the lake level went from 0.695 to 0.7092 and the forest's from 0.595 to 0.5676, the shares being the intent.

**Seven resources lie in it, in finite fields, and every one of them can be seen.** Iron, oil, stone, coal, copper and uranium lie in fields (`Resource`, `Deposit`): a cell holds a Poisson count of them by its land, each field a place with a number of sites — most small and a few huge, the floor of (1 − u)^−2/3 capped at 512, 2.52 on average — and whole tonnes that add up exactly to the cell's own total, which is drawn first; a field centred in the sea is drawn again, up to eight times, bar oil, because offshore oil is real. Forest is the forest of the terrain. Nothing has to be surveyed or found: the fields are in the world from the seed, the land office counts every one centred in an offer when it lists it, and the map draws them. The world's totals are counted once, in about 30 ms, and kept with the city, so that for each resource the world = what no city owns + what the city has left + what it has taken out, to the tonne through every purchase and every tonne lifted (`LandCheck`).
