What the city takes out is worked out in the order it bought the ground, the centre first, and forest grows back a 240th a month, though nothing cuts timber yet.

*The seven, as the world lays them (`Resource`); an offer's price counts only those with a good*

| Resource | Fields a km² of land | A site | A site holds | In an offer's price |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Iron ore | 0.2 | 0.0372 km² | 15 Mt | 1/350 of its world price, the $0.40 a tonne the office always charged against the floor of $140; a site is an Iron Mine's own ground, and a km² of land carries 7.59 Mt, the old listing's ore on a quarter of its sites |
| Oil | 0.02 | 0.0405 km² | 150,000 t | 5% of crude's since 0.7.62, by iron's rule of about a year and a half of a working site's profit; a site is a well's ten-acre spacing and thirty years of its 415 t a month |
| Stone | 0.01 | 0.1 km² | 13.5 Mt | free until it has an industry; a quarry 50 m deep |
| Coal | 0.002 | 1 km² | 6.5 Mt | free; a seam 5 m thick |
| Copper | 0.0005 | 0.5 km² | 300,000 t | free; the metal in 120 Mt of ore a km² at 0.5% |
| Uranium | 0.0002 | 0.1 km² | 200 t | free; 1 Mt of ore a km² at 0.2% |
| Forest | — | — | 13,700 m³ a km² | free; the terrain's forest, 31% of the land (FAO 2020) |

### Blocks, four sides and six places

**The ground is whole blocks** (0.7.67; `LandGrid`, `CityLand`; Jerus's design of 7 October). A block is a square of one grid lined up with the world, 2^k plots a side: 120 m at level 2 (`LandGrid.MIN_LEVEL`, 0.0144 km², the smallest block that holds one of the old 100,000 sq ft blocks, Jerus's *"one block smallest"*), doubling to 983 km at level 15 (`MAX_LEVEL`), so that blocks nest in the world's tiles (level 5, 960 m), its districts (8, 7.68 km) and its cells (11), and the world, 23 × 2^15 plots across, divides into whole blocks at every level. **The city's level** is the largest block of which six fit across a square of everything it owns (`LandGrid.levelFor()`, `FACE_BLOCKS`), so each of a side's six places is one block wide or two: 120 m until the city's whole area passes 2.07 km², 240 m to 8.29, 480 m to 33.2, 960 m to 133, and a district's 7.68 km from 2,123 km², on up to 123 to 246 km at ten billion people. **The centre** is the ground a city is founded with: rings of whole blocks of its level round the site's block until their dry plots reach the 3,000,000 sq ft of the founding figure (`CityLand.found()`) — on the default world 21 blocks of 120 m, 0.3024 km² in all, 0.2835 of it dry and 0.0189 a lake, 315 dry plots where the figure is 309.7 — and the city owns what is drawn, 3,051,569 sq ft, 1.7% more than the figure, because the books follow the map. Nothing rolls into it. What the city owns in square feet is its dry ground; the water inside its land is its own too, the lake its water plants draw on and the sea a desalination plant needs ([utilities](#20-utilities--roads)). **What it owns** is a region quadtree over the world's plots, each node unowned, owned whole by one holding, mixed, or owned whole by several, holding the centre's blocks and then each purchase's rectangle in the order bought. A purchase claims only the plots no holding owns yet, so the tree is the same whatever its history, given its rectangles in order: it is never saved, and is rebuilt from them at load (`LandGrid.replay()`). It names a plot's owner in 18 to 49 ns, where the lanes took 47 to 56, and a city of ten billion bought evenly is three to four thousand nodes.

```
the city's level   the largest k, at least 2, such that six blocks of 2^k plots fit across √(every plot it owns)
a block            2^k plots of 30 m a side: 120 m, 240 m, 480 m, 960 m, 1.92 km … 983 km, lined up with the world
an offer           w blocks across and 2w deep against the city's edge, w = round(√plots owned / 6 / 2^k): one or two
                   // clipped by the offers standing, trimmed of what the city owns, held to 2:1; its ground the plots of it not yet owned
```

**Four sides, six places each.** A block's side is read from its centre, seen from the founding site: the larger of its distances east–west and north–south, a tie — a corner block on the diagonal — going to North or South; and its place is which of six equal ranges, left to right facing out, the ratio of its distance across to its distance out falls in, from −1 to 1 (`GridOffers.sideOf()`, `sidePlace()`). Each of the 24 places has one offer standing, or none while its side has no room for it (`LandMarket.OFFERS_A_SIDE`, six; Jerus: *"six offers a side"*). **An offer is a rectangle of whole blocks against the city's edge**, listed in four steps (`GridOffers.list()`). Its seed is the free block of the city's frontier — the side's blocks not wholly owned that hold or touch owned ground — in the place's lane and nearest the site, ties to the lane's middle; with none, the side's free frontier block nearest the lane's middle; with none at the city's level, the same one level finer. Round the seed it is w blocks across and twice that deep, the long side outward, which the level makes one block by two, or two by four where the side has room (`DEPTH_OVER_WIDTH`), and never wider than a sixth of the side's frontier. Where it meets a standing offer, the columns on that offer's side of the seed go, or the rows from it out; then outer rows and columns the city already owns whole are trimmed, and it is held to 2:1 either way. Its ground is the rectangle's plots the city does not own yet, so a coarse offer takes in the finer steps beside it and no gap is left that cannot be offered. A new default city lists 19 offers, four or five an edge, each 1 × 2 blocks of 120 m and 0.0288 km², nearly a tenth of the city, with five places waiting, and all 24 stand within its first four to twelve purchases, as the design measured it on three worlds. From a square kilometre on, the offers bought average 2 to 3% of the city, and by the design's count Jerus's old city's size is 195 to 344 purchases and ten billion people 512 to 785, where the lanes took 411 to 444.

**Never rerolled.** An offer stands at its rectangle, its contents and its price until it is bought, and buying it claims exactly its rectangle's free plots, as one more holding, and lists that place again before any other: its next is the innermost free ground of its lane — a notch the purchase left beside the city first, otherwise the next rectangle straight out. The other 23 never move, because standing rectangles never meet. A place with no room waits empty and is tried again after every purchase and every month, the place just bought first and then North 1 to West 6 (`LandMarket.listMissing()`), and none waits while its side has room for it, which `LandCheck` and the playtest's audit hold. **Corners** fill out the same way: a corner block on the diagonal is North's or South's, and the notches a corner leaves are nearer the site than anything farther out in their lane, so they are offered first and the city grows compact rather than in fingers — bought evenly, the design's cities filled 60 to 80% of their bounding box at every size past 75 purchases, and bought on one side only they grew as a stepped fan, 46 to 58%, where a plain straight-out rule had filled 42% on one side. Ids go out in the order places are listed, so the same city listing the same places sees the same offers, and the offers are saved whole. One over 70% sea stays listed, because sea is cheap, but is tagged MOSTLY SEA and is never the best.

**The books are the plots, exact at every size.** What an offer holds is counted once, as it is listed, plot by plot on the world (`CityLand.groundOf()`): its km² in all, dry, fresh, sea and forest, every field whose centre plot lies on its free ground, whole, and its forest's timber at 13,700 m³ a km². Nothing is sampled, where the lanes read 64 by 64 samples of a band, and the map counts the same plots, so the books and the map agree to the plot; the design had proposed sampling past blocks of 7.68 km, at up to 1.6% of an offer's dry ground on land and a few km² on a coast, and the decision of 7 October was the exact count. Three things keep it affordable: a tile the city owns whole is passed over; a whole tile it owns none of is counted once a world and kept, up to 65,536 of them (`CityLand.TILE_COUNTS_KEPT`); and a rectangle of 2,048 tiles or more is counted over the machine's cores in whole-number sums, the same on any machine (`PARALLEL_TILES`) — `LandCheck`'s 2,116 tiles in 130 ms on two cores and 189 on one. An offer's ground cannot change while it stands.

Until 0.7.57 nine plots were on offer at any time (`LandMarket.LISTING_SIZE`; earlier editions said ten), generated deterministically from the plot's own id, so parcel 47 was the same plot in every session and in every reload. Sizes were multiples of a floor that rose with how much the city already owned; 15% of plots were enormous tracts, and the tract was what made the listing worth reading. **From 0.7.57 to 0.7.66** the land was a square centre sized to the square foot and four sides of ten lanes, wedges fanning out from the site, an offer a lane's next band, forty in all, each sized by a multiple drawn from its id of a block or of 1% of the city, a mean of 3.81, and measured from 64 by 64 samples of its band. A lane bought often grew a finger out of the city, its curved bands were never whole plots, and testing a plot meant testing forty frontiers. That geometry is kept, read-only, to put a saved city on the grid (`LegacyLand`; below).

### Whole fields

Jerus: *"Yes whole iron fields as one offer, yes that means significant investment."* A field — every one of its sites and all of its tonnes — belongs to the one piece of ground that holds the field's centre plot, wherever its sites lie: the centre, one purchase, or while it is listed one offer. The holdings and the offers never share a plot, so they hold every field exactly once and the world's totals stay exact whoever lists what when. It was the design's rule at 0.7.57; from 0.7.58 to 0.7.63 a field was shared site by site among the ground its sites lay under, so that a new city could buy a single site of its founding field for about US\$5.3M; since 0.7.64 it is whole again, for every resource alike, and since 0.7.67 by the plot that holds its centre. A city converted from a save of 0.7.58 to 0.7.63 keeps exactly the sites it held of a field it held only in part, and that field's other sites go a site at a time to the ground that holds each (below). On the default world the founding field is 35 sites and 449 Mt, its centre 26 plots south and 13 east of the site, a few blocks past a new city's edge, and none of a new city's nineteen offers carries any iron: bought toward, the offer nearest it each time, South 2 lists the field whole after six purchases, one offer of about US\$180M against a founding treasury of D\$100M, and the land office's funding page sizes its bond to it. An offer's row says so — *"Iron ore: 35 sites, 449 Mt in the ground: every field of it centred in this offer, whole, paid for in its price."* — and the map's hover names whose a field is, since its sites can lie under another offer. The playtest's player buys its iron the same way since 0.7.64, and since 0.7.67 only when the field pays for itself (`LongPlaytest.ironWhenNeeded()`): when an Iron Mine would pay and every iron site the city owns has a mine, it takes the cheapest offer holding iron if the mines it could carry — no more than the field's sites and than the city could staff, each paying what the mining sector's screen says one earns — earn a month the level payment that would repay its price over the funding page's twenty years at the market's rate (`fieldEarnings()`, `fieldPayment()`), out of the cash when that covers it and on that bond when the player's test for borrowing passes. On the grid without that test it bought the founding field at month 356 with 2,759 people, US\$206.2M on a D\$251.6M bond, and ended the run with none of its 199 iron sites under a mine; with it, its first iron is West 2 at month 359, a six-site field of 76.9 Mt for US\$37.05M out of the cash, and over the run it buys four fields, none on a bond, and passes thirteen looks whose cheapest field would not pay back. At 0.7.64 its first had been East 7 at month 485, a one-site field 33 plots out for US\$6.16M, and at 0.7.62 a shared site in month 32.

### Two prices, moved by different things

```
what the world asks   US$0.70 a sq ft × the world's price level × the crowding premium      // since 0.7.55; the player reads US$7.53 a m² since 0.7.68
an offer's price      that on its dry ground, 45% of it on fresh water and 8% on sea, + its fields' tonnes × their share of the world price × the world's price level, to US$5k, fixed at listing
what the city pays    the offer's dollars at the day's rate
what businesses pay   the local base × the crowding premium × a scarcity multiplier from 0.65 to 1.90 on allocated/available
                      // the local base struck at the expected price level since 0.7.42 (LandMarket.getBasePricePerSqFt()); the dollar base is the world's
the crowding premium  1 + 119 × s,   s = 1 / (1 + (4,000 / d)^5.3),   d = people a km² of the land the city owns
```

The multiplier passes 1.0 at about 61% built — below that the city sells land at a loss, which is the intended cost of over-annexing. The earlier version multiplied by utilisation, which sat between 86% and 100% for 2,400 straight months, so "scarcity" was decoration. From 9 September the city was founded with a **\$3.5B endowment** — D\$2.5B in the treasury and US\$1B in the vault from 0.6.10 — enough for a coal plant at 41% of it, a works department at 400 points a month, a shed of material, and a bank standing on day one. Since 0.7.10 it is D\$100M and US\$25M, and the big works are borrowed for ([founding a city](#17-founding-a-city)).

**The premium is crowding, not size** (0.7.55). Jerus, of the scale study's proposal: *"Yes for land price do that"*. Until then it was 1 + .008 a block owned + .05 a thousand residents, linear in the city's size: a copy of his city ten times over saw its rents rise 3.9 times and lost 18% of its people in thirty months, and at ten billion people a square foot would have cost about 19,500 times what it cost him. A city's size is not what makes its ground dear; how hard it presses on it is. So the premium reads the city's people a square kilometre of the land it owns (`LandMarket.peoplePerKm2()`), through a curve fitted to the three cities held so that each was quoted on the day about what its size had given it — city600 3.67 to 3.74, city2400 35.07 to 35.99, Jerus's 103.39 to 104.00: 1.65 at 1,500 a km², 60.5 at the midpoint of 4,000, 117 at 8,000, and never past 120, where the size premium had no ceiling (`CROWDING_MIDPOINT`, `CROWDING_STEEPNESS`, `CROWDING_CEILING`). A copy of a city K times over, K times the people on K times the land, is quoted exactly what the city is. **And the dollar price follows the dollar's own inflation** (Jerus: *"usd inflation not domestic inflation"*): the base times the world's price level (`WorldEconomy.getPriceLevel()`) times the premium, so the city's own inflation reaches it only through the rate — in Jerus's old city the dollar price rose 14.4% on the day, US prices having risen 1.137 times since his founding. What businesses pay keeps the domestic anchor, because ground inside the city is a domestic thing bought with domestic money: one price would have put every swing of the rate into every business's ground, and would have cut his businesses' by 47% on the day, his currency standing about 1.9 times above parity. The two prices meet at parity, so the city's margin on land is the currency's distance from parity and the scarcity, nothing else, and the land office names the price's parts. Crowding is a consequence and not a cause, as 0.7.58 measured: a city kept short of ground is crowded and quoted dear, but with the premium held at one the playtest's city grew slower, not faster.

### Land is bought in dollars

Jerus: *"when you buy land, make it so that it costs USD not domestic currency, and basically how it would work is a little toggle at the top to choose, when you buy land, to use up your USD reserves or to convert cash into usd exactly to buy the land, and the default is that you convert."* Since 0.7.6 the land office prices every parcel in US dollars — the same base and premiums, so at the founding rate of 1.00 every number is what it was — fixed when it is listed, and the treasury pays usd × rate on the day it buys: a weak currency makes land dear and a strong one cheap. What businesses pay the city stays local money, struck exactly as before, so the city's margin on land carries the currency, and a currency reform no longer clears the office's board. There are two ways to pay, a chip pair at the top of the office. **Converting**, the default: the treasury buys exactly the dollars and hands them over in one movement, and the vault ends where it began. **From the vault**: the dollars leave it and no local money moves, a capital transaction like the defence's, and the treasury's journal carries the land back against the budget's land line. A vault too short for the plot spends what it holds and converts the rest, and the receipt says so. On the default seed on 28 September the advisor paid US\$10.2B abroad for land over 151 months, none of it out of the vault, and it cost D\$6.15B at the day's rates, 39.6% less than it would have at the founding rate; on 1 October it paid US\$10.6B over 149 months, none of it from the vault, for D\$5.95B, 44.1% less; and on 5 October, at 0.7.49, US\$14.7B over 166 months, none of it from the vault, for D\$3.99T, 26,961% more than at the founding rate, its currency having drifted with prices that rose 1,213-fold; and at 0.7.64, on the world's land, US\$33.1B over 141 months, none of it from the vault, for D\$3.91T, 11,704.5% more, prices having risen 775-fold; and at 0.7.68, on the block grid, US\$30.3B over 84 months, none of it from the vault, for D\$8.17T, 26,870% more, prices having risen 1,001-fold.

Since 0.7.13 the office speaks the paying currency and square kilometres — Jerus: *"for the land … instead of blocks, say km^2, and add a button to buy multiple"*. A plot's large price is in local money when converting and in US dollars from the vault, with the other as a caption beside it; areas read in km² on the exact international foot, to three figures, so a block is 0.00929 km², and so do the build screen's *Not enough land* page and the time-skip report. Since 0.7.26 the office leads with square feet, to three figures (*9.68M sq ft*), with the km² after them, and the left panel's LAND header reads *N free · D\$x/sq ft*, only its Owned and Free lines in km²; since 0.7.61 it reads square kilometres again — the city's size, each offer's and its price a dry km². **Since 0.7.68 every area the player reads**, here and on every screen, notice and line of the log, is in square metres under a hundredth of a square kilometre and in square kilometres from there, three figures, grouped from a thousand (`LandManager.areaWords()`, `M2_WORDS_BELOW`): a House's plot *743 m²*, a new city's offer *0.0288 km²*, ten billion people's dry ground *1,760,000 km²*. The unit is picked after the rounding, so nothing reads *10,000 m²*, and a part reads in its whole's unit, *0.0288 km², 0.0273 dry* (`partFigure()`). Ground prices read a square metre — THE WORLD ASKS about *US\$7.53/m²* at founding, where it read US\$0.70 a square foot — and so do INVESTORS PAY, the margin, the price's parts, History's Land line and the city panel, while an offer keeps its price a dry km²; the farms' ground under cultivation, which read acres, reads the same way, and the investors write *no land - needs 5,570 m², 3,900 m² free*. The model keeps square feet and prices a square foot, so nothing it decides moved: the playtest's figures stayed byte for byte, and only its houses' words changed. The year book's land price stays a square foot, labelled, as the model's own series. A plot the city cannot afford no longer refuses: its button opens a funding page — converting, the twenty-year bond sized to the gap and the six-month note; from the vault, a twenty-year dollar bond or a six-month dollar note sized to the dollar gap, whose dollars are held in the vault, or the old top-up from cash as a third card; with the window abroad shut, a red card across two columns with the reason, and only what remains. Since 0.7.26 the page is the office's own, *Land office › Funding*, with the rail lit, a summary bar of what is held against the gap and a *short by* pill, and the offers as cards (`Pieces.offerCard()`, which Build › Funding took up in 0.7.40), and it goes back to the office when a month lands and nothing needs funding. And *Buy the next N plots*, five by default, buys the office's first N, cheapest ground a square foot first, and since 0.7.61 is *Buy the best N*, from every side; because a listed offer's price is frozen, buying them at once costs exactly what buying them one by one does. **Since 0.7.34 every Buy is a button that says its price** in the money the toggle pays in, the card's width: *Buy · D\$1.0B*; outlined, *Buy on credit · D\$1.0B*, when only a loan pays; from the vault and short, *Buy · US\$200.3M* with *the vault is short: ways to pay* under it; *Buy the next 5* the same in its line, and not drawn with nothing listed; and the funding page's offers *Buy 5 plots · D\$9.8B* over *issues the 20-year bond, then buys* — or *issues it abroad, then buys from the vault*, or *takes what the vault has and converts the rest*. A double-click buys one plot: until 0.7.34 the second click bought the card that had slid into the first one's place. Converting for land has never pushed the currency, which is on the list. Since 0.7.22 the player's hand on the queue reaches the ground too ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)): a stopped shell and a demolition on site hold their ground, a finished demolition's ground comes back to the city as free land, and a buy-out pays the owner for its ground at the price businesses pay the city, recorded as a buyback. Land purchases are not on City History's lane of decisions, as build orders are not; a big one the treasury borrowed for shows as the borrowing.

**Ground is what a mature city runs out of** — land sits at 88–90% for the last decade of most long runs, and the 2,400-month playtest city measured at 0.7.26 was 95% used or more in 120 months of 120 with no sector waiting, which is why no screen colours the share used any more — and the newest sectors are the hungriest for it. A Rail Terminal is 5,500,000 square feet, nearly three times a Coal Power Plant and the largest footprint in the catalogue; a Livestock Farm is 120 acres, the dearest ground of any farm at $108k an acre; a Metro Line is 30,000 square feet for thirty thousand journeys a month, five hundred times a gravel road's capacity per acre. That ladder is the whole reason the modes exist — see [transport](#21-transport--vehicles). Every sector's planner assumes the ground is free and none of them can see they are bidding for the same land; that is on the list.

### The office redrawn

Jerus, of the screens still to be done after Build: *"the others are still full of text and the design could be more intuitive and fun"*. The land office was the first redrawn in Build's style (0.7.26), and it answers top down whether the city has room to grow and which ground to buy. **THE GROUND** is four cells — the ground free, who is waiting, what the world asks and what investors pay — over the ground as one bar, the free ground solid and the next N plots as numbered ghosts, on a scale of the two together so that the bar always reads. GROUND FREE takes NEEDS YOU's GROUND row's colour, amber at 9,290 m² or less, an old block of 100,000 sq ft, and red at none (`CityNeeds.ground()`), and so do Build's LAND FREE and the left panel, whose *Land* alert shows only at none: never the share used, which sits at 95–100% for centuries with nothing wrong, so a red USED at 90% went. What the world asks is the going rate, the listing's median a square foot, read a square metre since 0.7.68 (`LandMarket.goingUsdPerSqFt()`), and who is waiting is read from the sectors the month found blocked (`Game.getLandBlockedSectors()`), where it had matched the words *no land* and missed a sector whose ground went between its plan and its purchase. **ON OFFER**, until 0.7.61, was the nine as a three-by-three of wide cards — from 0.7.57 the best nine of the forty — the next N numbered with a pink edge, each with tags of its own: BEST VALUE on the first, the cheapest ground a square foot with any ore inside its price, which is not `bestValue()`; MOST ORE on `richestDeposit()`, since 0.7.57 `richest(IRON)`; ORE and NEW; and one card can carry BEST VALUE and MOST ORE. Prices are neutral, red only when no way pays without debt. Under them four cards say what the ground is worth — the margin, the ground on top of the build, the ore and who is waiting — and behind *details* the world's price of ground over the city's life. The receipt is in the screens' money, *for US\$101.8M, converting D\$72.0M of cash at D\$0.7072*, where it printed *US\$101,800k*. Nothing the office said is gone: what is not on a card is behind an (i). `LandCheck`'s last section, since 0.7.26, holds the model reads it rests on: the going rate the median, the upper middle on an even count and nothing with nothing listed; the GROUND row's level its free ground's, word for word the row NEEDS YOU lists, a city 90% used still fine; and the receipt.

### The office round the map

Since 0.7.61 the office is laid round the city's map. The hero row is the map, 600 by 400, the city's land and its offers hatched over the world, with *Expand* to lay it over the whole window (below); and beside it **THE CITY**: its size in km² — in Jerus's old city as 0.7.61 read it, *107.8 km² · 89.6 dry · 0 fresh · 18.2 sea* — and its share of the world's iron, *of the world's 1.12 Pt of iron, the city owns 0.0000452%*; the four sides as chips, each with its cheapest dry ground a km² and BEST VALUE on the best's side, and since 0.7.69 a side that lists fewer than six naming its count, *North · 4*; and the chosen side's six places as rows of 28 pixels, each its place, 1 to 6 under *#* where it said *lane*, its km², its dry ground, fresh water and sea as one bar, its deposits as *8 · 136 Mt*, its price in the money the toggle pays in, its price a dry km², one tag — BEST VALUE, then NEW, MOST ORE and MOSTLY SEA, the first that holds — and *Buy*, or *Fund* when only a loan pays. Since 0.7.69 its size's tooltip gives its blocks, *1 × 2 blocks of 120 m · 0.0288 km² · 0.0273 dry, 0.0015 fresh*, and opens the row's; a place waiting for room is one muted row, *no room on this edge yet: it lists when the city grows here*; and the (i) gives a block's side in kilometres from one, *245.76 km*. A row lights its rectangle on the map, and a click on the map picks a side or an offer. Under them THE GROUND and its ghosts, *Buy the best N*, the worth cards — the ore card is *Ore and oil* — the details and the funding page are as they were, the funding page sized to the offer: converting, its bond is quoted for exactly what the chosen offers cost at today's rate less the treasury's cash (`Game.landCashGap()`), and from the vault for what the vault is short of their dollars, and once it is issued the Buy buys them. The 0.7.26 value bar went for want of room in a row. **Build buys from the same office** (`Game.bestOffer()`). LAND FREE reads its area, with *Buy the best: West 1 · 0.0288 km² · US\$215k ›* under it on a new city, naming its place since 0.7.69 where it read *Buy the best land*: the most dry ground a dollar among the offers the city can afford that are not mostly sea, the nearer on a tie. The no-land page's *Buy the best* takes the cheapest offer that covers the shortfall with bare ground, no ore to pay for, and says so — *"West 1, bare ground with no ore to pay for, covers the 743 m² short"* — or, with none, the best value, and asks again; a building short of ground has not asked for ore, and on the literal rule, the cheapest offer that covers it, the playtest's village was sold two sites of iron for US\$11.4M where bare ground cost a tenth of that, and stood still for two hundred months. The no-deposit page's *Buy the cheapest* takes the cheapest offer holding the ore, since 0.7.64, as the playtest's player does, where from 0.7.61 it took the most sites a dollar; and the no-coast page the cheapest offer with sea. Short of cash, each opens the office's funding page sized to that offer. And since 0.7.77 automatic building buys by the no-land page's rule for its own orders, bare ground only, paid as the toggle says ([automatic building](#22-the-screen)).

**Iron is a pooled resource.** Until 0.7.57 a parcel carried a deposit *count* and a tonnage the office drew for it, and roughly 28% of ore parcels carried more than one site; since then the sites and the tonnes are the world's fields in the ground the city owns. The sites cap how many mines can stand, one a site, and every mine draws from one reserve, what the city's fields held less what has been taken out (`LandManager.getIronReserveTonnes()`), worked out in the order the ground was bought. Ore in the ground is worth a fraction of what it fetches once it is out — the value is in getting it out, which is why it sells at 1/350 of the world's floor — and a deposit that is worked out closes its mine inside a year, which is what makes the bust when a mining city runs dry a real event rather than a slow leak. Oil is the same since 0.7.62, a well a site.

### The map of what the city has

Since 0.7.60 the city keeps a map (`CityMap`), and since 0.7.61 it is on screen. **What it stores** is not a picture but a count: each type's buildings in each 7.68 km district of the city's land, with the district's free plots and the iron and oil sites the city owns in it. Each month, once the month's construction and demolitions are done, each type's change goes into the first district with room — nearest the founding site first, but farms, utilities, mines, the railway and the car plants farthest first — removals the other way round, and nothing placed ever moves; mines and wells stand on the city's own sites of their resource, the first not worked out in the order the ground was bought. The map is drawn the first time anything asks for it, so a city nobody looks at pays nothing, and it is saved beside the city as `slot-NN-map.bin`, deflated, with its stamp in the save; a load whose sidecar is missing or stale draws it again, and the picture shifts once. **What it draws is what the city has, no more and no less** (0.7.64). Jerus: *"a brand new city shows that it has a few houses and a shop when it doesnt"*. A new default city holds one building, the Commercial Bank it is founded with (`Game.foundingBank()`), and no road, where 0.7.60's map had drawn homes from its people and workplaces from its jobs, the bank as a shop, beside two highways of the world's. Every building the model has is drawn once, as its own type, on whole plots sized to its type's land — the square root of its plots across and the rest down, a House one plot, Low-Rise Apartments two by three, an Iron Mine six by seven, a Livestock Farm 23 by 23 (`BuildingVisual.footprint()`) — turned to face its road, a mine on its own site; and the model's roads are laid as their own plots by kind, a Gravel Road 46, a Paved Road 26 and an Elevated Highway 7, and no others. A tile is painted from the seed, its ground, what is owned, what it was dealt and its neighbours' roads (`TilePainter`), so it looks the same every time it is drawn: from 0.7.64 to 0.7.71 buildings of sixteen plots or more first, then the roads, grown from ports the next tile agrees on and bridging fresh water but never the sea, then the rest, each from its own hashed place beside a road; since 0.7.72 its district's plan first and its roads one network (below). One that no free box on its tile can hold is drawn smaller, and counted: 7 of 2,340 in Jerus's live city at month 416 at 0.7.64, and at most a tenth on the densest screen `MapCheck` draws — 9.30% of it at 0.7.69; 16.72% at 0.7.71, the resized childcare having taken away the one-plot daycares that filled it; and 7.18%, 1,107 of 15,422, since 0.7.72, a tile dealt buildings to no more than 90% of its room while another tile has some (`CityMap.TILE_FULL_MOST`), so that a tenth is kept for the shapes buildings come in, and a large building laid on the grid's blocks near a road. A year on, a new city's map is its eleven houses, its store, its diner and its bank.

**The roads are one network** since 0.7.72 (Jerus: *"to make the map generation prettier"*), planned once a deal for each district (`CityMap`, THE NETWORK). Its road tiles are grown from the tile nearest its core, its mines' tiles joined first, while its main streets take no more than half its road (`MAINS_SHARE`), the rest the grid among its buildings. A tile's main street runs on its first or its last grid line, 4 or 28 plots in, by its column's own hash (`TilePainter.MAIN_AT`), leaving 27 plots open beside it, room for a Rail Terminal or a Livestock Farm; its mains cross at its hub, and an arm runs from the hub to each edge's crossing — the plot nearest the main line where it, the plot inside it and the two across the edge are dry, owned and no mine's, so both tiles read the same pair, one crossing an edge where one to three hashed ports had been. Inside a tile the grid's streets lie eight plots apart, so a + junction is eight houses from the next, Jerus's *"about 8 houses' length"* (`JUNCTION_APART`); lanes leave them in T's, and a fill comes last. Every road plot is laid before the small buildings, a rail yard or a large building is placed only where it leaves the network the room its roads still need (`keepsNetwork()`), and a building stands within four plots of a road (`REACH`) unless its tile has no room for it near its own roads. A district's highway is one straight run from its hub along its main row, turning only at the sea, the city's edge or a mine, four times at most (`CityMap.TURNS_MOST`), and crossing once, at the hub. **The railway is drawn**: the Rail Spur and the Freight Line as track, plot by plot, on its tile's edge away from the main, one line a district, crossing a street but never running along one, in openstreetmap-carto's rail grey, #707070, dashed white, on decks over fresh water up to a highway's fourteen plots; a Rail Terminal is a yard beside it on the track's tile nearest a mine. On Jerus's old city of half a million, laid on the design's square city, `MapCheck`'s eighth section draws 19,995 road plots in one piece, 135 + junctions none nearer than eight plots, each district's highway one straight run, 7,644 of 7,700 buildings within four plots of a road and none of the rest where its tile had room, and every one of its 792 plots of track. The sidecar is format 4 since, and an older map is drawn again once. **Since 0.7.77 gravel bridges rivers** (Jerus: *"gravel road bridge rivers sure"*): a street crosses fresh water gravel as paved, up to six plots, 180 m, the mockup's paved bridge (`STREET_BRIDGE`), every district's main streets may bridge a river where only one with paved road could, and a bridge is gravel where its tile has no paved road left, drawn as every bridge is, the road in its own colour over the deck; the hover says *Gravel road, a bridge*. The sea is still bridged by nothing. Jerus's live city at month 416 draws its roads in two pieces, where 0.7.71 drew 27 and 0.7.72 four — the streets north of its river join the rest, and a twelve-plot patch that touches it only at a corner stays apart — and the playtest's at month 1,000 in one, where they drew 34 and four, and at 4,000 in seven, where they drew 295 and eight, the rest a sea channel and slivers.

**On screen** it is one canvas (`ui/MapView`, its arithmetic in the model as `MapFrame`, `LandMap` and `MapTiles` so that `MapCheck` holds it): small in the land office and, with *Expand*, over the whole window, where a drag pans, the wheel zooms by 1.25 a notch at the pointer from the whole world to 16 pixels a plot, + and − zoom, 0 fits and Esc closes, with a legend, the Railway in it since 0.7.72, and a hover card — the ground, whose it is, an offer's size and price, the fields under it and their tonnes, the building, the road or the railway, and whether it is a bridge. It draws at the mockup's levels: painted tiles from 3.2 pixels a plot, at 4 pixels a plot and at 8 past 6; blocks of four plots from 1.4; blocks of eight below that while the view holds no more than 1,024 tiles; and past that the districts as tinted nodes over the world's ground. Tiles paint a few a frame, at most 8 ms of it, the middle of the view first and another level's picture standing in; a month or a purchase stamps the tiles in view again and repaints only those whose stamp moved; and its caches together stay within 48 MB at the design's size, 47.8 measured. The first draw is made off the screen's thread, on a copy of the city's land and counts, and taken back on it caught up to the month (`Game.mapDraft()`, `adoptMap()`). **Its cost follows the screen, never the population**: a 198-tile screen paints and rasters in no more than 80 ms with Jerus's old city as it is and at 9,814, 10,000 and 19,629 times it — five and ten billion people — 59.5 ms at worst at 0.7.64 and 63 to 68 since 0.7.72's network, each within 1.5 times the five-billion copy's, and a month's change at five and ten billion costs no more than 5 ms. Room is counted plot by plot, about 8 ms a district, and only in the districts a purchase touches, but a large save loaded without its sidecar counts every district once. **On the grid** (0.7.69) every line of the overlay is on whole pixels: the city's edge is one shape of whole straight runs, crisp and stepped, a pixel inside its ground; its block lines are faint, white at 8%, where a block is 6 pixels or more (`MapFrame.BLOCK_LINES_FROM`); each offer is hatched and edged on its free ground only, because a coarse rectangle takes in the city's finer steps beside it and those had read as ground on offer — 16 of the 24 round Jerus's converted city hold some of his ground — and numbered by its place on its freest square at least 11 pixels each way (`PLACE_LABEL_FROM`); and an offer larger than the view is drawn over all of it, where 0.7.61's test of its corners had dropped it. The outline and the cut-outs are found once a purchase or a listing, not every frame, and `MapCheck` holds the arithmetic. The view has not yet been seen in the game's own window; what has been looked at is the painter's renders, and for 0.7.69 a mirror of the overlay drawn in Java2D — a new city, the playtest's at months 1,000 and 4,000, and Jerus's autosave converted — and for 0.7.72 and 0.7.77 the painter's renders of the network, the track and the bridges on the same cities and Jerus's live one.

### Older cities on the grid

Every save written before 0.7.67 is put on the grid once, as it loads (`LandConversion`, `GridConversion`), and no money moves for it. **A save of format 31** (0.7.57 to 0.7.66: a centre and forty lanes) has its old ground read as it was, through the lanes' geometry kept read-only (`LegacyLand`), and snapped to whole blocks one level finer than the city's offers — 240 m for Jerus's live city, whose offers are 480 m. Its fields decide first: each whole field's centre plot and each site of a field it held only in part, a save of 0.7.58 to 0.7.63, marked as the city's or not. A block holding both kinds is split into its four, down to the plot if need be; otherwise a block is the city's when a point in it is the city's, not when a point in it is another's, and else when the save owned half its plots or more. What comes out is one holding, the converted centre: its sites and tonnes the save's to the bit and what it has taken out as saved, so no field changes hands, and a field held in part keeps exactly its own sites (`landPartFields`); its five areas the plots drawn, so the books follow the map and the city's square feet become its dry plots; its purchase records kept as history, what it paid on record — Jerus's, 133 purchases, US\$125.2M listed and D\$164.3M paid — and nothing charged for ground the snap adds or refunded for ground it takes. Then 24 offers are listed round it, the one time offers are listed afresh, at the prices the save last struck, after the load has put back the prices, the buildings and the allocation, so they are priced on the converted city's crowding. Jerus's live city, his autosave at month 416 and slot 3 at month 212, gains 0.130 km² of dry ground, 1.8%, and 0.015 of lake, and loses 0.078 of sea; three blocks are its for its fields, one split; the two fields it held in part keep their 6 of 8 sites; and its 13 iron sites and 160.6 Mt are the save's to the bit, its cash unchanged. Played twelve months, saved as format 32 and loaded, both come back to the bit in every pool the money audit reads, and play their next month alike.

**A save of format 30 or older** (before 0.7.57: one figure, a pool of iron and nine parcels with no place) is given a world as it always was: its seed, if it has none of its own, made from its name, its founding treasury, its ground and its month ([founding a city](#17-founding-a-city)); its site found as a new city's is, with one test more — the square holding its ground must be at least 80% dry, with the sea within half its side and 2 km — over the 64 coastal cells nearest the middle, failing all of which the driest site found. Since 0.7.67 its centre is rings of blocks of the city's level round that site, the last split down to the plot, holding its dry ground to within a plot and never less; its iron is its own, the sites it had or at least its mines standing and on order, and exactly its tonnes, none invented and none yet taken out, with a field laid at least 1 km out on its own dry ground if the world put no iron there; and the other resources are the world's fields centred on it. Jerus's old city holds its 89.63 km² of dry ground in 960 m blocks to within a plot, with 2.1% more sea and 12.6% less forest than its 0.7.64 centre, and keeps its 155 iron sites and 508 Mt; city600 holds its 3.03 km² in 240 m blocks with a legacy field of ten sites, and city2400 its 33.29 in 960 m blocks; and the old city, played twelve months to 514,354 people, saves as format 32 and reloads to the bit. Since 0.7.59 a save with no water rights is given what its fresh plants already pump less what its lakes yield, so that loading idles nothing it had — Jerus's old city 300,000 units, having no lake in its centre, city2400 960,000 and city600 none ([utilities](#20-utilities--roads)). A save whose square feet disagree with its land by more than a plot — a copy of a city K times over, or ground set by hand in a harness — has its land drawn again round the same site to hold them, as an older save's is, its iron and what was taken out kept (`LandConversion.restate()`).

## 19. The catalogue

*Seventy-six buildings in `buildings.json`, hot-editable next to the game, every one on a sourced real capital cost at the size the game actually builds it. Edit a number, restart, look — no rebuild. Ids are permanent, because saves are keyed by them; the next is 76. Eighteen were added in the three days to 18 September, and three since 0.7.54: the Desalination Plant (0.7.59), the Oil Well and the Oil Refinery (0.7.62). Since 0.7.71 three old ids are childcare centres of new sizes (below).*

| Category | Templates | What it does |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Residential | 3 | House (six), Studio Apartments (two), Low-Rise (four) — a home has a size and a household has to fit it |
| Commercial | 3 | Convenience Store, Small Grocery — coverage is how many people can shop — and the Commercial Bank |
| Industrial | 5 | Industrial Bakery and Bakery, which buy crops and bake bread and bakery goods out of them (until September 2026 they were a Textile Mill and a Food Processing Plant making a good called Food out of nothing); and the eleventh sector's Meat Works, Snack & Oils Plant and Bottling Plant — five, six and four posts, among the smallest investor-built job steps in the catalogue |
| Heavy industry | 6 | Steel Foundry and Steel Mini-Mill, plus manufacturing's Fabrication Shop, Fabrication Works and Machine Works — the first domestic customer steel ever had — and since 0.7.62 the seventeenth sector's Oil Refinery, 8,300 t of crude a month cut since 0.7.76 into 580,170 litres of petrol, 1.4 million of diesel and 7.7 million of four products it ships, where it made 8.3 million litres of fuel |
| Business services | 3 | Contact Centre, Shared Services Centre, Engineering Services Office — seats sold abroad; the last needs licensed engineers before it will open |
| Agriculture | 4 | Mixed Farm, Grain Farm, Greenhouse Complex and, since 16 September, the Livestock Farm — 13.8, 55, 3.4 and 120 acres; the glass is the one that survives expensive ground, and the herd is the dearest of the farms per acre — $108k against the Grain Farm's $22k — and sells 6.5% of its build cost a month against the Grain Farm's 18% |
| Mining | 2 | Iron Mine — sixty jobs, a quarry lifting 30,000 t/yr — and since 0.7.62 the sixteenth sector's Oil Well, three posts lifting 415 t of crude a month; each stands on a site of its own resource that the city owns |
| Construction | 2 | Construction Depot, and the Construction Materials Plant — the seventh sector's only building |
| Electricity | 2 | Coal Power Plant — 280 MW at $1.43B, far more than a city of 74,000 needs — and a Wind Farm, the first small plant beside it |
| Water | 2 | Water Treatment Plant, which treats no more than the city's lakes and river yield since 0.7.59, and the Desalination Plant, the same water from the sea at twice the cost and 10,880 kW |
| Infrastructure | 6 | Gravel Road, Paved Road, Elevated Highway — each the cheapest per trip over its life across a band of land prices, and since 0.7.70 a gravel road can be paved — and since 16 September the Bus Network, Light Rail Line and Metro Line, the same ladder two rungs on: 2,500, 8,000 and 30,000 journeys a month, and the first things in this category that ever had a payroll |
| Rail | 3 | Rail Spur, Freight Line, Rail Terminal — 50,000, 200,000 and 500,000 tonnes a month across the city boundary at $140M, $520M and $1.24B, owned by the twelfth sector and financed like a steel mill; a terminal is 1,482 jobs on 5,500,000 square feet, the largest hiring commitment and the largest footprint in the game |
| Automotive | 4 | Vehicle Works and Assembly Plant (120 and 500 cars a month), Commercial Vehicle Plant (150 vans), Locomotive Works (four wagon sets) — all fed on fabricated steel and machinery, and anchored on heavy manufacturing's revenue per head rather than the food plants', because the first draft never cleared the interest test |
| Luxury | 2 | Boutique and Department Store — 320 and 4,200 pieces a month over a counter, importing every one of them |
| Hospitality | 2 | Diner and Restaurant — 13,500 and 40,500 meals a month, each buying the Convenience Store's basket scaled to the person-months its meals come to, to the kilogram |
| Healthcare | 14 | childcare, general, senior and death care, on Build since 0.7.24 as four rings, the picked ring's buildings as cards; since 0.7.71 childcare is three centres, 80, 220 and 360 places |
| Education | 9 | three basic stages, college, university, and four professional schools that each license one job |
| Safety | 4 | two police buildings and two prisons — the city pays for all four |

Every building declares a cash cost, construction points, materials, maintenance, capacity, lot footprint in square feet, electricity and water draw, road load, its job mix across eleven types, and — since the template — **which sector owns it and what it makes and uses**. A healthcare building also declares what it treats, a school what it teaches, a safety building whether it is a station or a cell block, a transit line the journeys it can carry and a rail building the tonnes. The road load is one number and it is read as three: fitted to the catalogue itself, 0.726 × jobs + 0.878 × homes + 0.0386 × tonnes a month, so a mine keeps its 420 and learns that 68% of it is ore, a university is all commuters, and a shop's freight is a van at a back door. Money throughout is in thousands: a cash cost of 30 is $30,000, at founding prices, and since 0.7.42 struck every month at the price level the city expects ([the anchor](#15-the-central-bank)). Every building prices itself — sticker and all-in, from the same method that charges, since 0.7.19 with its labour at today's builders' wages and their sales tax in it — on a card that explains it from its own numbers.

**The Build tab files it differently.** The table's categories are `BuildingType`'s, and since 0.7.24 Build files the catalogue in fourteen of its own (`BuildAdvice.categories()`): the city's five — Utilities (electricity and water), Roads & transit, Healthcare, Education and Safety — then, after a rule, the market's nine — Homes, Shops, Industry (industrial, heavy industry, mining and construction), Offices, Farms, Rail, Vehicles, Luxury shops and Restaurants. Five were renamed as Jerus chose, *"Yes, rename them"*: Residential is Homes, Commercial Shops, Industrial Industry, Infrastructure Roads & transit and Business services Offices, on Build's strip alone. Since 0.7.25 the market's pages draw their buildings in their owning sectors' groups: Industry's seven, nine since 0.7.62 — food mills, food processing, steel, fabrication and machinery, iron, oil, refining, building materials and the builders — and Shops' two, the groceries and the bank's branches. `BuildAdviceCheck`'s first section holds that every building sits in exactly one of the fourteen.

### One card for every building

Jerus: *"also the build card for every building, i think the card itself needs a redesign dont you think?"* Since 0.7.25 every one of the 73, 76 since 0.7.62, is one card, 300 pixels wide (`BuildCard`), the city's five and the market's nine alike: the head, an icon square in the colour of who builds it, *you have N* and what is on site with its wait and a link to the site; the tags; a hero that says what the building gives the city in its own verb and unit, with a detail line; *$X all in · sticker $Y*, always both; two bars scaled within its group — the first the price a unit of what it gives, or for the makers, farms, mines and vehicle plants how many months of value added at today's prices it takes to pay for itself, an office's months of its exports, and since 0.7.70 a road's its cost over its life a trip it takes off the road, and the second the land a unit on market cards and on a road's since 0.7.70, the posts it could not fill per 10,000 served on the city's, and of 100 posts how many the city could not staff on offices — with no track in a group of one; the investors' line, on market cards; the needs line — posts, *the city could staff N%*, the land and its share of what is free, *runs $X/mo*; the stepper with +10 and +100; the quote and its verdict; and the (i) with its stat cover. A tag goes only to the strictly best on a bar, and only in a group of two or more. Each group's note reads the sector's own figures — the doors, the shops' coverage, the counters, the kitchens, the rail's trade, each maker group's demand and nameplate. The quote warns of a missing deposit, *no iron deposit* and since 0.7.62 *no oil deposit*, a missing coast, *no sea owned to draw* (0.7.59), or a licence, *nobody licensed*, before the click.

**The investors' line** says *on site* when an investor's order is on the site, and otherwise the sector's word for the month, read since 0.7.30 into one of twelve kinds ([the private sector](#8-the-private-sector)), then in amber *this one:* and the first gate this building fails now, in the order the build path asks them — the deposit, the licence, the staffing test, the land, a loss in the estimate; a click opens the owner's Investors page. The words are the month's and are not saved, so after a load or a founding the line says nothing was recorded until a month runs. **Build is a button that asks to be pressed** since 0.7.34 — Jerus: *"everywhere you have build, like the build button, it should be more intuitive aka like an actual button that is basically asking to be pressed, cause currently its a tiny text"*. It is the card's width under the stepper and says the order, *Build 3 · $37.5M*, the count and the quote's all-in total; outlined, *Build 3 on credit · $37.5M*, when the treasury is short, a press opening Build › Funding ([the city's borrowing](#13-the-citys-borrowing)); grey and saying why when it cannot go ahead — *No land free* or *Short 743 m² of land*, *No iron deposit* or *No oil deposit*, *No sea to draw*, *Nobody licensed to work in it* — with the way out under it and a press opening the page that explains; and at none *Build · choose how many*, where a press chooses one and prices it and never orders. A double-click is one press. It had been a small grey button beside +100, disabled at none. Since 0.7.41 a city card's figures are served, supply over demand, under one verdict ([the screen](#22-the-screen)). `BuildCardCheck` holds the cards in ten sections, without a screen: every building has a card and a unit; the hero and the bars are the model's; the tags; the notes; the investors' line and its gates, each caused by a fixture in the build path's order; the verdict; since 0.7.30 the word's kind; since 0.7.40 a run of orders priced as placing them in turn would be; and since 0.7.41 served. The cards have not been seen rendered.

### Childcare in three sizes

Jerus: *"one city had 5k daycares and 2k residential buildings, hilarious, the numbers children and housing wise make sense ... i think we need to resize those, daycares are childcares and childcares are even bigger"*. A Home Daycare, eight places for $147k, was the cheapest place to put up, so the advice ordered them by the hundred and Build's cards tagged it the cheapest a child; his live city held 629 of them beside 1,521 home buildings, and the test player, which builds no childcare, had never shown it. Since 0.7.71 the three childcare buildings are centres on the same ids (`buildings.json` and the built-in twins, which `BuildingDataCheck` holds equal), each figure on the model's own scale curve through its two old centres — price, upkeep, power, water, land, road load and posts — with ten points a place and 40% of the price material, so a place costs less to build, keep, stand on and staff the bigger the centre:

*The three centres (0.7.71); a place's price is its cash and material at founding prices*

| Building | Places | Was | Posts | Land | A place | Children an adult |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Small Childcare Centre (15) | 80 | Home Daycare, 8 | 20 | 2,917 m² | $27.4k | 4.0 |
| Childcare Centre (16) | 220 | Neighbourhood Daycare, 60 | 53 | 6,503 m² | $24.9k | 4.15 |
| Large Childcare Centre (17) | 360 | Childcare Centre, 220 | 84 | 9,606 m² | $23.7k | 4.29 |

The sizes are sourced: 80 is the most a Quebec childcare installation may take (*Educational Childcare Act*, CQLR c. S-4.1.1), about Ontario's largest groups one room each (O. Reg. 137/15, Schedule 1: 79); 220 is the model's own old centre, figure for figure; and 360 is China's guide for a kindergarten (Kindergarten Work Regulations, 2016, art. 11: generally not more than 360 children). Every centre's staffing lies between Ontario's three adults to ten children and one to eight. A save holds its buildings by id, and Jerus's word was *"keep them as they are"*, so a Home Daycare loads as a Small Childcare Centre with its places, posts and ground, ten times what it had ([open questions](#25-open-questions)); id 16 is called a Childcare Centre because it is that building now, so an old log line naming one still reads true, and nothing maps names back. The advice sizes the order to the need, the whole order over the places lacking ([the screen](#22-the-screen)), while a card's first bar, the quote for one with the yard's material free, still tags the Small centre the cheapest a child where the yard holds material. The map draws a centre as care, where it drew a Home Daycare as a home. The test player builds no childcare by default; its rule, the advice's card whenever NEEDS YOU lists childcare, is a flag (`-Dplaytest.childcare`), and with it on the playtest's city at month 4,000 held 2,951 Home Daycares and 183 Centres for 2,123 home buildings at the old sizes, and 12 Centres and 235 Large ones for 2,379 at the new. `ChildcareCheck` holds the three ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

> **Both halves of a price are sourced now**
>
> A unit of construction material was \$2,000 and is **\$18,000**, defined by the House: ten units against a real house's \$180,000 of structure. Every template's split was re-derived at a real material share — 40% for a building, 25% for a plant, 60% for a road — with every total held to the dollar. It also found that the builders' material import bill had never been paid: \$2.75bn crossed the border over 4,000 months and the expense struck at zero, so Construction ended every run holding the money and the balance of payments never saw a unit move. Range runs from a Mixed Farm or an Oil Well with three posts — a Home Daycare with two, until 0.7.71 — to a Rail Terminal with 1,482 jobs, the Regional Medical Centre's 996 the largest the city pays for, and the terminal's 5,500,000 square feet the largest footprint in the game, ahead of the Livestock Farm and a Municipal Cemetery's 2,000,000.

## 20. Utilities & roads

### Power and water

The grid starts with 10,000 kW free and the reservoir with 8,000 units of 10,000 gallons. Both are gated by the same utility workforce. Power is $10 a kilowatt a month and water $50 a unit — the model's .01 and .05, in thousands, as the Services books print them, and about $5 per thousand gallons. Since 0.7.28 power reads in kW, MW and GW (`Money.power()`) on Services and Build, and the console's utilities report in kW, where earlier editions and the report said watts.

**Only businesses are invoiced.** Houses, depots, roads, the water plant's own 900 kW and the city's own buildings all draw power nobody pays for, and since 0.7.28 that unbilled draw is split into the homes' (`UtilitiesHandler.getHomesElectricityDraw()`, `getHomesWaterDraw()`) and the city's own buildings'. Booking revenue on the whole city's draw was money from nowhere scaling with the housing stock — 73% of it, measured. The utility books exactly what its customers' statements charged them, not a recomputation at the end-of-month ratio. The plants are the city's own: what they sell less their wages goes into the city's cash each month, and a loss is paid as the city's services promise (`TreasuryLine.CITY_SERVICES`). **Since 0.7.41 both read served**, supply over demand, unclamped, under one verdict: green at 100% or more and off NEEDS YOU's list, which for the networks means past 133%, the inverse of the 75% the dashboard has always called tight; red at or under 100%; amber, *tight*, between ([the screen](#22-the-screen)). A city drawing 43% of its plant reads 233% served, enough, and one at 124% of capacity 80% served, short.

### Roads

The city starts with 400 units of capacity — the streets that already exist. Traffic flows freely to 90% of capacity and degrades after that, floored at 35%. Three roads, and the land ladder was in the catalogue before anybody pointed at it: a gravel road is 500 square feet per unit of capacity, a paved road 208, an elevated highway 42 — twelve times the capacity per acre for two and a half times the money. Since 16 September the load is three streams and the network can be relieved by a highway, a tram or a train, but never deleted; that is [transport](#21-transport--vehicles), and this is the baseline it is measured against. Since 0.7.70 each is weighed over its life, and a gravel road can be paved (below).

```
throughput = 1                      if load ≤ 0.9 × cap          // FREE_FLOW .9
           = max(0.35, 0.9/util)   otherwise                  // MIN_THROUGHPUT .35
served     = cap / load the curve reads                  // since 0.7.41: flow is 1 from 111% served, and 0.9 × served under it
```

The road is written as one pair everywhere since 0.7.29, in whole per cents, and since 0.7.41 as served rather than full: *62% served · 56% flow* where it read *161% full · 56% flow*, the same fraction the other way up. Its red line is the curve's own, 111% served, where the flow starts to fall, so a road 100–111% served is red and *tight* where the networks go red at 100%. Since 0.7.29 the room before it slows and its spare capacity read the load the curve reads, where they read the raw trips: 585 trips of room on a road 161% full.

Congestion slowing the sites is the pointed part: a jammed city builds the roads that would unjam it more slowly, and the floor is what keeps that from being a trap.

### A road over its life, and a gravel road paved

Jerus: *"the game still recommends gravel roads, even when i think paved roads are better, also ... make it an option to upgrade from gravel to paved, but not from paved to highway, and that the build menu allows and recommends this if better, total cost is higher than just building paved"*. What had recommended gravel was not the advice, which has priced a road's ground since 0.7.51 and in his city picked paved roads, but Build's road cards, whose price a trip left the ground out, so that *cheapest per trip* went to gravel in every city — in his, 17.9 D$k a trip against paved's 31.5 and a highway's 45.6 — and the test player, which ranked the roads by their founding cash cost a trip and built nothing but gravel in the 0.7.69 run, 123 orders. Since 0.7.70 one figure decides all three: **a road's cost over its life, a trip it takes off the road** (`BuildAdvice.lifetime()`).

```
over its life      its quote + its ground at the land office's price + a month's running × the annuity
a month's running  repairs at 1% a year of what it costs to build today, the builders' tax in, + its power and water
                   at the utility's prices + a line's posts and upkeep − a month of fares from the riders it adds
the annuity        240 months, the funding page's 20-year bond (LIFE_MONTHS), at that term's real rate
a trip             over its life, over the trips it takes off the strained line, its freight grade in them
```

The advice ranks its six road candidates by it, the three roads and the three lines; a road card's first bar is it, *cost per trip over 20 years, with its land*, and its second the ground a trip, tagged *cheapest per trip over its life* and *least land per trip*; and the test player picks its road by it. **Over its life gravel gains, not loses**: its repairs are a share of its smaller price, so the cheaper road is the cheaper to keep, and the life moves the line toward gravel. In the cities measured a paved road beats it where a gravel road's 450,000 sq ft of ground is worth about 1.4 to 1.7 times its quote, and a highway farther out. In Jerus's city at month 416 that line sits at 0.95 of what his land office charges, so paved already wins there, six Paved Roads at 56.7 D\$k a trip against gravel's 57.8; in city2400 it sits at 1.05 and gravel wins, 18.30 against 18.60; the playtest's city at month 4,000 would need its ground 1.89 times dearer, at month 1,000 5.55 times, city600 11 times and a new city 15. So gravel stays a young city's road. In the playtest the road move orders paved roads from its look at month 3,422, 8,074 D\$k a trip over their life against gravel's 8,627, and the city ends with 592 gravel roads and 77 paved, where at 0.7.69 it stood 661 gravel and none.

**A gravel road can be paved** since 0.7.70, one or many at a time, and a Paved Road is not raised to a highway, as Jerus asked (`ConstructionControl`, F; `Game.paveRoads()`). The price is a Paved Road's work and the take-up of the old surface at the demolition rule's 5% of the gravel road's work, and a Paved Road's material less the gravel road's 193 units, which go into its bed, the builders' tax in (`Game.quotePave()`), paid from the treasury's cash with no loan page. So a gravel road and its paving cost more than a Paved Road built outright — 17.6% more in Jerus's city and 22% in the playtest's with the yard empty — while paving one costs 75 to 79% of a new Paved Road where the material is bought; on a day the yard holds a gravel road's material and not a Paved Road's, the two quotes can sum lower, because a quote takes the yard's material free. The pavings queue on the Paved Road site as the city's order, standing on the gravel roads' ground: each gravel road carries its 900 units until its own Paved Road opens, first in first out, and then retires, its Paved Road carrying 1,200 and the 200,000 sq ft between their grounds coming back free. A paving site is not stopped while it paves ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)), and the hand is saved with the rest of the queue's, an older save having none. It is recommended only where it beats a new Paved Road over its life a trip, the ground it frees taken off at what the next road would pay for it (`BuildAdvice.pavingBeatsPaved()`): the Gravel Road card's PAVE TO A PAVED ROAD block tags it *paving beats a new Paved Road*, the Overview offers *Gravel Road, paved* as a card of its own and leaves it out of *Build all three*, and the test player paves where paving is the least of its roads. In the default playtest it never is: of 0.7.69's 140 road orders with gravel to pave, it would have beaten a new Paved Road at none. `RoadCheck` holds the life, the crossovers, the cards, the price, and paving played, saved and refused ([how it's checked](#24-how-its-checked)).

### Fresh water has a limit, and the sea can be drunk

Since 0.7.59 the Water Treatment Plants together treat no more than the city's lakes and river yield: 121,600 units a month a km² of fresh water the city owns (`UtilitiesHandler.FRESH_UNITS_PER_KM2`), plus its water rights. The yield is the world's renewable river runoff, about 42,700 km³ a year (Shiklomanov), over the world's river and stream area, 773,000 km² (Allen & Pavelsky 2018): 4.6 million m³ a month a km², which is 121,600 units of 37.854 m³. So a water plant's 60,000 units need about half a km² of lake or river. The reservoir's 8,000 units are groundwater, the old wells', and stand outside the limit. Past it the rest of the fresh plants' nameplate idles and the water is rationed through the same ratio as any shortage, which throttles the businesses that draw it; under it, what the plants make is the old formula to the bit.

```
the limit    121,600 × owned fresh km² + the city's water rights
water made   (8,000 + desalination's nameplate) × fill + min(the fresh plants' nameplate × fill, the limit)
             // fill: the utility workforce's, as before; at no fill at all the wells still give their 8,000
```

The Services page says so in amber under the water bar — *"fresh water limit: 62% of the plants' nameplate idle · buy lake or river, or desalinate"* (`CityNeeds.freshLimitLine()`) — and holds its *at full staff* to the limit, and the build advice values a fresh plant at the water left under it, so a capped city is offered desalination. **The Desalination Plant** (id 73, `"source": "SEA"`) makes what a water plant makes, with the same crew and ground, at twice its cost, the low end of seawater reverse osmosis's two to five times a conventional plant; and it draws 10,880 kW, 3.5 kWh a cubic metre against the water plant's own 0.29, the biggest single new draw on the grid, 1.34 wind farms of it. The limit does not reach it, and it needs the sea: an order with no owned sea is refused, *No sea to draw* (`BuildResult.NO_COAST`), and the refusal's page buys the cheapest offer with sea ([land](#18-land)). **Rights** keep the old cities whole: a save from before the limit is given what its standing fresh plants already pump less what its lakes yield, so that loading idles nothing; a new city has none. A new default city owns 0.0189 km² of lake since 0.7.67, its whole blocks taking in a little more of it than the old centre's 0.011, a limit of 2,298 units, so its first water plant, 60,000 at nameplate, would idle 96% until it bought lake or river; at 0.7.59 the playtest's city had 1.1 km² of it by its first shortage, bought with its ground, and at 0.7.64 it was never offered a move past the limit, ending with 16.68 km² of lake and river, two water plants and none for the sea; nor at 0.7.68, ending with 69.16 km² of lake and river and 197.01 of sea, two water plants and nine desalination plants. The playtest's player orders a water plant only while the water left under the limit covers it, and then desalination on owned sea, the offer with the most lake or river a dollar (`LandMarket.bestFresh()`), or the cheapest with sea.

### Construction output

```
round(working capacity × construction fill rate × road ratio × health work ratio)
working capacity = the city's own 400 points + the depots' capacity × the share of their posts offered   // since 0.7.17
```

One definition, used by the screen, by the sites, and by what the sector is paid for. The three had to be the same number: a copy that drifts books revenue for work nobody did, and very nearly did when roads arrived. What reaches the *sites* is what is left once the standing stock has had its repairs — about 40% of the total, permanently — and since 0.7.17 it is shared among them by the crew each building can use ([the builders](#9-the-builders--the-queue)). The depots count at the share of their posts the builders kept on that month, and the city's own works department, which has no posts, counts whole; whoever is weighing an order reads the same figure with every post offered (`getConstructionOutputAtEveryPost()`), because an order is work and work hires the crews back. Since 0.7.22 a rushed site's crews work longer hours on top of it, more points in their first two months and fewer from the third, and the builders count them beside the output.

## 21. Transport & vehicles

*Until 16 September the entire transport model was one scalar: a road network with a capacity and a load, one throughput ratio between 0.35 and 1, and three road types that were the same road at three prices. Jerus:* "decomposing the existing import/export bands into world price + transportation cost… then later, transportation efficiency can make that freight component smaller or larger." *Nine batches followed in three days under the same version number, each one there to make the next possible: the band decomposes, the load splits, the modes and the fare, the railway, the vehicles, and the screen that finally shows a player any of it.*

### The band was a freight bill

Every traded good carried two constants and the gap between them was the whole local market — and nothing in the game said why the gap was the width it was. Each good carries a third number now, the cost of moving one unit, and the two ends split into four:

```
worldImportPrice = worldBuyPrice  + baseFreight     // the world's own ask, plus getting it here
worldExportPrice = worldSellPrice − baseFreight     // the world's own bid, less getting it there
```

Three quarters of the wedge is freight and one quarter the world's margin, and the split is a game decision rather than a measurement: it sets how much of the band good logistics can ever win back. At three quarters a 23% band bottoms out near 6%. **The price table was already a freight model and nobody designed it that way**: freight as a share of the world price sits at 21–25% for fifteen of the seventeen goods that had both ends, and the two outside that band are iron at 49% and materials at 43% — the two lowest-value-density things in the game, where real freight genuinely is half the delivered cost. The delivered prices are the stored literals and the world band is derived, which is the opposite of how it reads and the only way round that is exact: storing the world band and adding the freight back gives 0.8470000000000002 for steel and 0.27999999999999997 for crops, and an ulp in this codebase is never nothing. Not one price moved on the day it shipped, and eight seeds over 333 years came back byte-identical; `TradeCostCheck` asserts every delivered price against a table of what it was that morning, because a test that reads its own subject proves nothing.

### One road load is three

`Traffic { COMMUTERS, GOODS, BULK }`, and which mode can carry what falls out of the classes rather than needing a table of exceptions: commuters can ride a tram and nothing else can; goods — a shop's bread and milk — are a van at a back door however many rails a city lays, and take the train only across the boundary; bulk — ore, steel, crops, grain, aggregate, beams, machines, a locomotive on a low-loader — is what a railway is for. The shares were fitted rather than guessed, by least squares against the catalogue itself:

```
roadLoad = 0.726 × jobs + 0.878 × homes + 0.0386 × tonnes a month        // R² = 0.74 over the 56 templates that loaded a road when the fit was struck; seventy do today
```

The implied rate is one worker per nineteen tonnes a month — a truckload — and nobody set out to encode that. The residuals are all explainable and all one way: an Iron Mine 280 over the fit (heavy vehicles), a Penitentiary 288 under and a Long-Term Care Complex 136 under (their occupants do not commute), a University 258 over (students travel and the fit counts only wages). None of it matters, because the fit supplies the *share* and the stored road load supplies the *magnitude*: a mine keeps its 420 and learns that 68% of it is ore.

*Commuters / goods / bulk, as the fit reads the catalogue*

| Building | Road load | Split |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Steel Mini-Mill | 500 | 17% / 0% / 83% |
| Grain Farm | 18 | 14% / 0% / 86% |
| Iron Mine | 420 | 32% / 0% / 68% |
| Bakery | 40 | 53% / 16% / 31% |
| Small Grocery | 55 | 87% / 12% / 1% |
| University | 520 | 100% / 0% / 0% |
| A played city | — | 86% / 3% / 11% |

A real city is 86% people, which is what urban traffic actually is. And the ensemble found a defect whose fix is the better design: the first version summed the three streams to get the network's total, and eight seeds came back subtly different from the build before them — a thousand dollars in three trillion, one person in forty-eight thousand — because every building's three loads add to its own road load to the bit, and what does not survive is adding them up in a different *order*. So the total keeps the exact sweep it always had and the breakdown is read alongside it. The demand did not change; only the ability to see what it is made of.

### The modes, and a fare that is a price

*The land ladder, per unit of capacity — a journey a month for the transit lines*

| Mode | Capacity | Land | Sq ft a unit | Cash a unit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Gravel Road | 900 | 450,000 | 500 | $2,584 |
| Paved Road | 1,200 | 250,000 | 208 | $4,500 |
| Elevated Highway | 1,500 | 63,000 | 42 | $6,400 |
| Bus Network | 2,500 | 20,000 | 8 | $4,800 |
| Light Rail Line | 8,000 | 45,000 | 6 | $8,000 |
| Metro Line | 30,000 | 30,000 | 1 | $10,667 |

A metro is five hundred times a gravel road's capacity per acre for four times the price a journey. A city that has run out of ground and not out of money builds one; a city with ground to spare never should — which is the first real answer this game has had to its own late-game wall. **Every mode is a relief on an unchanged baseline**, and that is the design rather than an implementation detail: a city with no highway and no transit computes exactly the load it computed yesterday and degrades on exactly the curve it degraded on. A highway relieves freight, not by carrying more but because a tonne of ore on a grade-separated road does not share a junction with a school run — bulk by 40%, goods by 15%, commuters not at all. Transit takes people off the road entirely, and three things stop it being the answer to everything: a city's lines reach 65% of each group of commuters, the car-less and the car owners alike since 0.7.49 (`TRANSIT_MAX_SHARE`), so no more than that ever ride, whatever is built; what transit can carry is capped at twice the road capacity under it, because buses are road vehicles and a metro station needs a street outside it — *a city that builds a metro and no streets gets a metro nobody can reach*; and it never touches freight. Measured on a load of 10,000 in the played mix: 5,590 riders with room to spare, 4,800 with fewer streets, 800 with none, and with the best of everything **the road still carries 39%** of what it would. The road can be halved and it can never be deleted. It is also why the stream split matters to a business: an office and a mill on the same jammed road read 74% and 47% against the road's own 42%, because the mill beats the road by exactly as much of its own traffic as rides the tram, and a lorry in a jam is in a jam. A sector with nothing standing reads the city's own blend rather than a clean road, because the planner costs a first plant at the sector's operating rate and a congested city was cheerfully building plants a 38% road said it could not afford.

**A fare was a price, not a charge**, from 16 September to 0.7.48. Nobody chooses to be policed and a patient in a clinic is not shopping; the person on a bus chose to be, and can choose a car instead. So the ridership ceiling was what a *free* system would carry and the fare walked it down on a straight line to nobody at the maximum: free, 5,590 riders; at the default, 5,311; at the ceiling, none. And the two lines moved against each other, which was the whole decision — six times the fare took $58,695 a month instead of $13,276 and put 1,398 more cars on the road. Jerus asked for a dial that can be made profitable *"by alot"*; it can, at a ridership the city may not want. The fare is money, so a reform moves it — the twenty-third of that family and the first caught in the same edit that created the field — and since 0.7.47 the curve reads the dial in founding money through the currency's unit, so a reform moves nobody's mind about the bus; until then it did, by about 5% of the riders in the 2,400-month city divided by a thousand, and its cap is the founding cap in the new unit (`TaxPolicy.maxTransitFare()`). Since 0.7.42 the fare is real: the dial is set in founding money and charged at the price level the city expects (`TaxPolicy.chargedFare()`), so it keeps its worth, and the screens show it in today's money. Two things were found on the way: nothing in the infrastructure category had ever had a job, so nobody had written a line to pay one, and a Metro Line is 828 posts; and the fare was charged once a month against a constant that says *a single journey*, so a monthly pass cost $2.50 against a $3,460 wage, seven hundredths of one percent, and the buses could not have paid for themselves at any fare a player would set. That was the transit loss the list had carried as a balance problem. It is 40 journeys a month now — out and back, twenty days — a pass is $100 or 2.9% of an unskilled wage, and the dial stays per ride because that is the number a person on a platform recognises.
